title: Oxford names next town manager, announces clerk-treasurer will stay with town
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford names next town manager, announces clerk-treasurer will stay with town

 December 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News

 OXFORD — After nearly half a year without a town manager and a controversial hire that never actually made it into the Oxford Town Office, the Commissioners of Oxford have found a new town manager.Holly Wahl, currently the Chesapeake Beach Town Administrator, will begin the role on Jan. 6
During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, Commissioner Katrina Greer read the news to residents.
The commissioners also announced at the meeting that the town's Clerk-Treasurer Vickie Sharp will be staying in her position and will not leave the town for other employment at the end of the year, which Sharp had told the Star Democrat in late November.
"I think we all want to thank Vickie for the work she did in the last month and a half with nobody in the office to talk to except herself," Commission President Norm Bell said.
Residents in the audience of the meeting clapped upon hearing the news, and at the end of the meeting, one resident reacted to the news and the tone of the meeting by saying it felt like the best Christmas present.
According to a news release from Oxford, Wahl has served Chesapeake Beach as its town administrator for the last eight years. In that time, she helped reduce town taxes more than 17% while increasing services to citizens and businesses, reduce liabilities by $9.44 million, increase the town's net position by over $21 million and improve the town's fund balance by over $15 million, the news release said.
Wahl attributes those improvements in Chesapeake Beach to fiscal accountability, the acquisition of grant funding, the implementation of organizational changes, the application of technology and the alignment of staff with mission-critical activities to eliminate inefficiency, according to the news release.
During the meeting, Greer said the commissioners are "delighted" that Wahl will be joining the town.
"I mean, we think this woman is going to knock it out of the park," she said.
In the news release, the commissioners said they think Wahl's experience in procurement and in managing larger projects will bring the town "cost savings with better management."
"Ms. Wahl has experience applying for and managing grant monies, coordinating with state and local agencies and has worked with the Army Corps of Engineers on major waterways projects such as the $3 million federal dredging of Fishing Creek Channel," the release said.
Along with town management, Wahl's experience includes operations director roles in both the private and nonprofit sectors. According to the news release, Wahl holds business administration degrees from the University of Maryland and Johns Hopkins University. Wahl is currently finalizing her dissertation to obtain a doctorate in public administration and public policy from George Washington University.
At the meeting on Tuesday, Bell acknowledged the months-long search it took to find a new town manager.
"It was a learning experience," he said. "And I think we wound up with a very good pick."
In late June, Michael Calvert — a former city administrator in Liberty, South Carolina — was hired to fill the role of town manager, which former Town Manager Cheryl Lewis was retiring from. But just three days after the commissioners announced the hire, they announced that the town and Calvert had "mutually agreed to part ways."
The commission did not comment on why the decision was made. Former Liberty City Council Member Peggy Edwards said she resigned from the council due to issues with Calvert and the city's mayor. She said that when Calvert was in the position, there was a lack of transparency and mismanagement of money.
The situation led to the commissioners choosing a search firm to assist in the search for the next town manager, which led to Wahl's hiring.

 EASTON — During Tuesday's meeting, the Easton Town Council approved four-way stops at two different intersections on Brookletts Avenue.Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh recommended the stop signs be added at the intersection of Brookletts Avenue and South Harrison Street, as well as the intersection of Brookletts Avenue and Hanson Street.
Van Emburgh wrote that the all-way stops will improve safety for pedestrians, bicyclists and drivers. By a unanimous vote, town councilmembers approved a resolution for the stop signs.
Currently, at the intersection of Brookletts Avenue and South Harrison Street, vehicles driving on Harrison Street do not stop, while vehicles traveling on Brookletts do.
Van Emburgh's recommendation indicated that Easton's crash data dashboard showed five crash incidents at the intersection occurring between 2018 and 2023. Three were "property damage incidents" and two were "injury incidents."
At Brookletts Avenue and Hanson Street, stop signs halt drivers on Hanson Street but not Brookletts Avenue. According to crash data, between 2018 and 2023, there was one crash incident involving five people at the intersection.
"I know that we've had multiple conversations and emails and stuff about some of the complaints of traffic and stuff on Brookletts," Interim Town Manager Alan Lowrey said Tuesday. "And this is an opportunity to try to address that to see if implementing these four-way stops will improve some of that accident data and speed concerns."

title: Easton, can you spare a dime for a paper bag?
author: MARION O ARNOLD
content:
Easton, can you spare a dime for a paper bag?

 September 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARION O ARNOLD | Section: Columns 
 
 714
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Easton Town Council President Frank Gunsallus has introduced an ordinance aimed at the town's Plastic Bag Law by doing away with the paper bag fee.The law prohibits stores from providing plastic bags and requires retailers to charge a 10-cent fee for paper bags. The fee helps retailers with the higher cost of paper bags. According to Maryland Retailers Association's Sarah Price, who testified at the last Town Council meeting, the 10-cent fee helps level the playing field between retailers allowing them to recover the cost of paper bags for shoppers who take them, reducing overhead and keeping prices lower for all shoppers. It's a fee, not a tax. Retailers keep the fee.
Paper bags come at an environmental cost, so the 10-cent fee also helps the law from inadvertently substituting one environmental problem with another. Paper bags require trees and a polluting process to make them. Paper bags can be recycled or composted, but most will end up in landfills where they become a source of planet-warming methane gas.
For shoppers, the fee makes things more equitable. Those shoppers who take paper bags pay for them. Not having a fee will raise prices on other goods since retailers will have to recoup the increased costs of giving out "free" paper bags. Those of us who bring our own bags will end up paying higher prices, even though we won't be using disposable paper bags.
Most importantly, the 10-cent fee incentivizes shoppers to bring their own bags. It's your choice. You don't have to spend a dime if you bring your reusable bags.
I think of major environmental laws like the Clean Air and the Clean Water acts. Businesses had to make big investments to meet the demands of the laws or meet up with stiff penalties and fines. Here, with our plastic bag law, we're just asking businesses to charge a small fee for paper bags and to keep every dime they collect.
Without the 10-cent fee the law loses a part of its environmental impact. No one is saying let's bring back plastic bags, but if free, paper bags will fly out retailers' doors — and smaller retailers will bear the cost. Laurel, Maryland, passed a bag law in 2022 without a fee. Two years later, they changed their law to add a 10-cent paper bag fee because more than two-thirds of shoppers there just took the free paper bags. Since January, shoppers in Laurel taking paper bags has dropped to 32%.
Easton's plastic bag law was the result of months of work by a team of town leaders, Easton residents, and community representatives, with encouragement and backing from Talbot watermen, local businesses and environmental organizations. Since then, plastic bags no longer hang from our trees, pile up in hedgerows and ditches, and end up in our waterways. The economic and environmental benefits for Easton are many.
Jeff Harrison, president of the Talbot Watermen Association, was an early supporter of the plastic bag law. He has said, "We have to understand, whatever we do on the land eventually ends up in the water." At the last town council meeting, he testified to the law's success, saying he "doesn't see bags in the water anymore."
The law works, and we can readily see the results.
Mr. Gunsallus argued that repealing the 10-cent fee was for those "who are struggling." I have no doubt that people struggle, but no one shopping in Easton is required to pay that 10-cent fee either. There's no fee if you bring your own bag. Bing Crosby's big hit from 1932, "Brother, Can You Spare a Dime?" came to mind. Back then you could go to a five and dime store and do some damage with that dime in your pocket. You could get two pairs of socks or two cups of coffee. Today, about all you can get for a dime is a brown paper bag.
Mr. Gunsallus does not take into account the greater cost of pollution from paper bags. It affects us, the creatures we share this space with, and causes economic and environmental damage. The 10-cent paper bag fee helps the plastic bag law work. Thanks to our enlightened town leaders, the law is a great success and a benefit to us all. As the old saying goes, "If it ain't broke, don't fix it."

author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com

11th annual Shop with a Hero builds lasting connections

 December 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 STEVENSVILLE — Community children fostered relationships with local first responders while picking up the perfect gift during the Kent Island Optimist Club's 11th annual Shop with a Hero event at Stevensville Target Dec. 14.Partnering one-on-one with a police officer or firefighter from surrounding agencies, over 60 children were selected this year to participate in the shopping extravaganza through recommendations from local schools.
Each child was provided $200 to spend as they pleased for everyone on their Christmas list, and creating unforgettable memories, the 11th annual day once again filled with smiles, laughter, and the true spirit of the season to connect the community.
Understanding, for most people, the only interaction they get with police is when something bad happens, and Shop with a Hero aims to build positive experiences and foster relationships between youth and see first responders in the right light, according to Kent Island Optimist Club President Jennie Hager.
The day provides festive spirit for children who might not otherwise be able to, alongside the community, for children, their families, and local first responders. Shop with a Hero has grown exponentially over the years and the group couldn't be more thrilled to be able to provide for local children, Hager said.
Along with generous community donations, the Optimist Club raises money all year round to completely fund the shopping expedition, including a lip sync battle at Cult Classic Brewing company in October, she said.
Back at American Legion 278, heroes, kids, families and the community enjoyed a hearty breakfast and photos with Santa and Mrs. Claus.
Participating hero organizations included the Queen Anne's County Department of the Sheriff, Maryland Transportation Authority, Queenstown Fire Department, Kent Island Fire Department, Maryland State Police, Maryland Transportation Authority Police, Centreville Police Department, Greenbelt Police Department, Maryland Department of Natural Resources,, QAC Department of Emergency Services, Grasonville Volunteer Fire Department, United Communities Volunteer Fire Department.
Also in attendance was the Kingsman Motorcycle Club, ready to step in and help cover any shopping costs needed.
"It's all about the kids," biker Bobby Deal said.
The likeminded community and youth focused mission of the American Legion provides the hall space and breakfast and countywide volunteers from various organizations lend hand in wrapping all the goodies.
"Everyone just jumps in, it's a total community effort," Hager said, "It never ceases to amaze me, it's the community coming together."

author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com

A spacious and welcoming place - Central branch reopens main floor following a year of renovations

 January 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 11 | Section: News

 DENTON - Following a year of renovating and redesigning, the central branch of the Caroline County Public Library at 100 Market Street in the county seat reopened its first floor space Dec. 18.The soft reopening is designed to help staff fine tune details as they welcome patrons and visitors. A grand opening celebration is planned when the new elevator is finished in spring 2024.
New carpet, neutral walls, fresh shelving and new furniture create welcoming decor in the more open spaces of the library's main floor. The main desk is bigger and moved away from the wall, making it easier for staff members to see most of the library's interior.
Bennett said she wanted people to experience the library as "bright, open and inviting."
"This is perfect," customer Romont Fletcher of Denton said Dec. 20 as he set up his laptop on the desk attached to an upholstered chair. He had not been in the library for a year and was surprised when he walked in. "This is a great renovation," he said.
"This is good space, and it's flexible space," Executive Director Debby Bennett said. "It's a well-built library." Bennett, who has been with the library since 1983, will retire in June 2024.
"In 1983, people came in, got their books and checked them out and went home," Bennett said. "Now people come to stay, whether it's work on our computer, hang out with their friends in the Teen Zone, a family comes in and spends time looking for materials and just spending time here, small meetings in the study room, research in the Maryland room."
The $2.1 million renovation project began Jan. 2, 2023. Bennett, the Caroline County Board of Library Trustees and library staff met their goal of reopening the first floor to the public before Christmas.
The central branch has experienced many changes in its 62-year history. Card catalogs and hand-stamping due dates have been computerized. Circulating books are still a staple, but today library card holders can check out a Cricut machine, sewing machines and even fishing poles.
The central branch has 13,739 card holders who can check out materials, but visitors can obtain guest passes to use the public computers.
As if to illustrate the changes, two days after reopening, four teenaged young men checked out software to play games on library Xboxes in the Teen Zone.
The renovation was funded mainly by two "highly competitive" State Library Capital Grants, Bennett said.
In addition to replacing the roof slates on the library's 1995 addition, the building underwent extensive first floor renovations.
Phase 2 includes improving the elevator in 2024.
The Phase 1 grant in fiscal year 2023 financed 79%, or $917,000 of the project.
The library board provided the local match of $244,000 from their John Hargreaves fund.
This phase included replacing three HVAC units at the end of their useful life, improving lighting, upgrading the emergency fire alarm system and phone system, enhancing electrical capacity for increased technology, removing the wall dividing the two children's rooms, providing a family bathroom adjacent to the children's areas, increasing seating capacity, improving sight lines and creating quiet areas. The improvements brought the library into compliance with ADA requirements.
The cost didn't include shelving, furniture and other additional costs that were incurred throughout the renovation, about $335,236. The library paid for those costs, except for $78,000 raised by the Friends of the Library for shelving for the adult, young adult and Maryland Room collections.
Phase 2 is being funded by a fiscal year 2024 State Library Capital Grant that pays for 78%, or $467,000, of the project, with the remaining $132,000 provided by the Caroline County Commissioners.
This phase includes replacing the elevator, which is "at the end of its useful life," Bennett said.
The new elevator will comply with ADA requirements and current codes.
The phase also includes replacing the addition's 4,000 square foot roof with artificial slate, which had deteriorated and become a "serious safety hazard," Bennett said.
The elevator provides access to public space, administrative offices and the third floor attic storage area.
"The (two-sided) main service desk is going to work a lot better for staff to both answer basic questions and check out items, and also to be able to work with people with more complex reference questions," Bennett said. "And also we have so much better visibility of the other desks and more areas of library to see who might need help (and) for security."
"Back in 1995 when we renovated and added on, we didn't have cell phones and laptops and iPads," Bennett said, adding that the internet was fairly new then.
"The MakerSpace used to be our reference area in 1995 with 7-foot shelves of reference books. Now, all the reference materials are online."
More square footage not taken up by books "frees up more people space," she said.
There's a lot to figure out," Bennett said. "Half our staff are new and didn't work down here. And for all the staff, it's a new layout. So it's a matter of figuring out procedures and ironing out all the little extra things. So opening like this without a big fanfare - and this is a quiet time of the year anyway - is giving us time to figure a lot so that things go smoothly for staff and customers."
"I've seen a lot of changes, but this library has always been innovative," Bennett said. "It's always been forward-thinking and also thinking: What does the community need? What does community need that they don't even know they need?"

title: Cambridge man found not guilty of murder in shooting last year
author: Konner Metz
content:
Cambridge man found not guilty of murder in shooting last year

 June 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 775
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — After just over an hour of jury deliberation Thursday afternoon, a Cambridge man was acquitted of charges in connection to the fatal shooting of 26-year-old Virgil Simms last year.Jo'Mir Norman, 18, was found not guilty on all counts, including first-degree murder, assault charges, and firearm and handgun charges. Family and friends of Norman embraced outside the court room. Norman's father, Joseph Norman, said his son was wrongly accused and said it was relieving to hear the not guilty verdict.
During the trial, Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard relied on video evidence to piece together Norman's whereabouts and the clothes she said he wore the day of the murder.
On Oct. 20, 2024, Cambridge Police Department officers responded to the area of Pine Street just after 7 p.m. for reports of a shooting. Investigators determined 19 rounds were fired by two different shooters. Simms was pronounced dead on the scene, sustaining a gunshot wound to the chest.
On Thursday, jurors rewatched videos that had been closely examined during the four-day trial. Leonard argued camera evidence showed Norman and the other shooter flee from the scene and enter a house on Camelia Street, where clothes allegedly worn by Norman the day of the murder were found by investigators.
But defense attorney Molly Fox told jurors that prosectors relied too heavily on circumstantial evidence and had glaring holes in their arguments, such as the fact that surveillance video meant to bolster clothing and vehicle evidence jumped from a 1 p.m. convenience store video to a 6 p.m. video an hour before the shooting.
Fox called the state's case against Norman "a circus" like she's never seen before.
"There was a lot they didn't even try and present," Fox said in an interview after the verdict was announced. "It just seemed like it was thrown together last second."
Fox cited a lack of direct witness testimony, missing videos and issues during the discovery process leading up to the trial as reasons why "the evidence did not point toward my client."
Prosecutors encountered some specific challenges during witness testimony.
On Monday, an EMT who responded to the scene testified that she saw Simms with a gunshot wound to the head, though it was established during trial that he sustained a chest wound. And during the trial, a state's witness who allegedly dropped off the two shooters the day of the murder did not confirm that Norman was one of the men she drove that day. Leonard called that witness "young" and dealing with a "very packed court room."
"Don't be fooled by the shaved head here today," Leonard noted to jurors, referencing Norman's buzz cut Thursday compared to longer hair he had when arrested.
Fox also reminded jurors of a key mistake in the early days of the murder investigation: Maryland State Police wrongly arrested then-15-year-old Brian Wongus Jr. at the same time they charged Norman in October.
Attorneys on both sides acknowledged police misidentified Wongus as one of the shooters. An MSP spokesperson said Tuesday that charges against Wongus were dropped in late October or early November.
Leonard said the evidence investigators used when wrongly charging Wongus was "very different" from the evidence presented against Norman at the trial. She said jurors received "no testimony at any time that Jo'Mir Norman was misidentified."
Fox said while video evidence can be useful, it can also lead to wrong identifications.
"You have nothing more than what they had when Brian Wongus was arrested," Fox told the jury.
The lead-up to Thursday's verdict and the reaction afterward was emotional but civil on both sides, with family of both Simms and Norman attending. When the trial began Monday, Simms' mother Yolanda Hernandez took the witness stand.
Hernandez provided a brief but emotional testimony as prosecutors asked her about her son.
Hernandez said she and Simms had grown closer since he had two young children. She said he liked to cook, grill and joke around. "He was a decent guy," Hernandez said.
Leonard told The Star Democrat after the verdict that she respects the jury but was "disappointed" in the outcome. She declined to comment further, citing an active case against the man police arrested after misidentifying Wongus, 19-year-old Jahmere Bryan.
Bryan, from Cambridge, faces the following charges in connection to the Simms shooting: first- and second-degree murder, first- and second-degree assault, use of a firearm while committing a felony, and three other firearm and handgun charges.
A May 19 hearing for Bryan in the Dorchester County Circuit Court was postponed. A jury trial is scheduled for next month, but Leonard said Thursday that trial is expected to be pushed back due to a change of Bryan's defense attorney.

author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com

Maryland stories: Legion, firefighters retire U.S. flags

 St. Mary's held a retirement ceremony of sorts during its 38th annual National Flag Day event on June 14 in Leonardtown.A total of 906 flags were burned.
The event marks the date in 1777 when the Continental Congress approved the design of a national flag, according to the Library of Congress. Flag Day became official in 1916 when President Woodrow Wilson issued a presidential proclamation to honor the Stars and Stripes every year on June 14, and in 1949 President Harry S. Trueman signed an Act of Congress designating a national Flag Day.
"I actually love this ceremony. It's humbling and it's patriotic and I absolutely love it," said Rep. Matt Morgan (R-St. Mary's), who added the event was the largest in the state. "I was reminded by how important ceremonies like this are when I was doing some research ... and a poll said that only 18% of young people were extremely proud of the country, and that's huge indictment on our nation's education system and social media. ... You look around and it's hard to believe but America's history is, although not perfect, if you're comparing it to perfection it's still pretty unique and special."
Commissioner Mike Hewitt (R) served as emcee for last week's event, which featured a procession of St. Mary's County color guards, remarks from dignitaries and the hanging of the POW flag by Paul Thorn of St. Mary's County ABATE of Maryland.
American Legion Post 221 of Avenue held a flag retirement ceremony, while Elks Lodge 2092 of California gave a history of the American flag.
"Flag Day to me means to preserve the flag, take care of the flag and when it's in disarray then we do the honor ceremony," said American Legion Post 221 Color Guard Capt. Rick Jennings, who added he thinks "a lot of people know about [Flag Day] but let it go to the wayside."
The cast from the St. Mary's Summerstock production of "Cinderella" performed the national anthem and the county song, and refreshments were provided by the Seventh District Optimist Club.
Residents can drop off unserviceable flags at the three St. Mary's County senior centers, three public libraries, the ACE Hardware stores in Charlotte Hall and Leonardtown or at the American Legion Post 221 at 21690 Colton's Point Road in Avenue.

title: Preston man sentenced to 15 years for stabbing
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Preston man sentenced to 15 years for stabbing

 February 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Crime

 DENTON — A Preston man was sentenced Thursday to 15 years in prison for the February 2022 stabbing of a then 25-year-old woman.Agreeing with a recommendation from the prosecution, Caroline County Circuit Judge Heather Price handed Mark William Thompkins a 30-year sentence with all but 15 years suspended. He will receive credit for 714 days, or nearly two years, already served, according to court records.
Thompkins, 26, pleaded guilty last October to one count of attempted second-degree murder.
Price also referred Thompkins to the Patuxent Institution, a treatment-oriented, maximum security correctional facility.
"I believe that it was an appropriate sentence," said Caroline County State's Attorney Sloane Franklin, who prosecuted the case. "Unfortunately, the mental health system is broken and failed both the victim and Mr. Thompkins."
Thompkins' defense attorney, Jesse Hicks, could not be reached for comment.
Thursday's sentence comes nearly two years after the young woman was stabbed near Holly Park Drive and Gilpin Point Road in Preston shortly before 3 p.m. on Feb. 17, 2022.
During the Oct. 30 plea hearing, Franklin said trash collection workers near the scene first saw the woman sitting in the driver's seat of her vehicle with a man, later identified as Thompkins, seated behind her.
Thompkins began striking the woman with his fists, then brandished a knife to stab her neck.
The woman ran from her vehicle and collapsed in the front yard of a nearby house. Thompkins cradled her while holding the knife to his own throat, Franklin said.
A witness attempted to help the victim, but Thompkins threatened them, pointing the knife at them and yelling for them to get back.
Multiple law enforcement agencies, including the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, Maryland State Police and Maryland Natural Resources Police, responded to the stabbing.
Franklin said Thompkins punctured his own neck with a knife while running to the woods to evade officers.
After 15 minutes and the use of multiple non-lethal methods, including a taser, a state trooper was able to knock the knife out of Thompkins' hand to detain him, police said.
Both Thompkins and the woman were flown to the University of Maryland Shock Trauma Center in Baltimore for treatment of their injuries.
After his arrest, a judge found Thompkins incompetent to stand trial in April 2022. He was committed to the Maryland Department of Health until August 2023, then transferred back to a local detention center upon being found competent, according to court filings.
Following his release, Thompkins will be placed on five years of supervised probation. He will also be required to complete mental health treatment.

 OXFORD — The time to approve budgets is right around the bend for the Commissioners of Oxford.At a town meeting Tuesday, the commissioners introduced an amended fiscal year 2024 general budget and heard from Town Manager Cheryl Lewis on a preliminary draft budget for fiscal year 2025.
At the previous town meeting on Feb. 27, Lewis said she always starts this time of year with going over amendments to the current budget.
"It's almost like a training session for the real budget for the public and commissioners," she said.
According to an amended budget document posted on the town website, the town's revised income for fiscal year 2024 is $5.57 million The original budget listed $6.33 million for income.
The town's revised expenses for fiscal year 2024 was $5.76 million. The original budget listed $6.59 million for expenses.
The revised net income is negative $183,560. On the original budget, the town's net income was listed as negative $252,465.
For fiscal year 2023, the town's revenues were $2.61 million and its expenses were $2.79 million.
At the meeting Tuesday, Commissioner Katrina Greer noted that the town had $120,000 more in investment income this year.
Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin said she was concerned that legal fees were $30,000 higher in the amended budget than the original budget for fiscal year 2024.
Lewis said legal fees are always estimated in the budget.
"When you have more legal needs than any other year, it's going to happen," she said. "In the last nine months, we've had more legal needs."
After introducing the amended budget, the commissioners scheduled a public hearing for April 23.
PRELIMINARY DRAFT
The Commissioners of Oxford also heard from Lewis about a preliminary draft budget for fiscal year 2025. Lewis went through different capital expenditures that the commissioners will need to consider as they begin the budget approval process.
"Those are the things you really need to pick through and decide what items you think you want to do," she said.
One budget item Lewis pointed out was $20,000 for improvements to the Community Services Building, where the Oxford Town Office, commissioners meeting room and Oxford Police Department are located. Lewis said these funds would go toward replacing the deck on the back of the building and painting parts of the building.
For the police department, Lewis pointed out $68,000 that would go toward replacing or purchasing a new truck for the department and toward furnishings needed for the office.
Lewis said she put $10,000 in the preliminary draft budget to purchase two AED units — one to be placed outside the Community Services Building and one to be placed at the ferry dock.
Lewis said the Public Works Department would like to trade in and upgrade one of its tractors. She said the cost would be between $70,000 and $80,000. Along with the tractor, she said public works has asked to get the shop painted.
Lewis said she added another $10,000 to the budget for public works that could be used to purchase a trailer or to purchase a few smaller items.
For the Roads Department, $150,000 is currently earmarked for a paving project that would include the post office and bank parking lots. Although this project was originally a part of the fiscal year 2024 budget, Lewis said the town would not be able to go out to bid, get a contractor and pay for the project before fiscal year 2025 begins.
Lewis said the Oxford Community Center — which is owned by the town — also asked to be included in this paving project so its back parking lot, which is currently gravel, could be paved.
Lewis mentioned a $100,000 optional budget item to replace water lines under the street. She said the town could earmark money for this in the event that it identifies a real problem.
For wastewater, Lewis highlighted a $200,000 budget item for a backup pump. Lewis also suggested incorporating $100,000 into the budget every year to pay for water lines and sewer lines on an alternating basis. She said this had been set up before the COVID-19 pandemic, but hadn't been continued.
Lewis said she will come back to the commissioners with a date for a budget workshop so that the budget can be adopted by May 31.
In a text, Lewis said the goal is to adopt the budget 30 days before the start of the new fiscal year, July 1.
"It is always possible to have the process carry past that date," she said. "I try to set it up so the commissioners understand their target dates far enough in advance to keep things on schedule."

title: Naked truth about Lakeside: It's based on a lie
author: DAN WATSON
content:
Naked truth about Lakeside: It's based on a lie

 February 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAN WATSON | Section: Columns 
 
 2168
 Words 

 Read News Document

 So here is the naked truth about Lakeside that everyone now knows: Talbot County's approval of that huge, billion-dollar subdivision was based on a bald lie, fictitious and as empty as the weavers' loom that wove the emperor's new clothes.Contrary to what was represented by the developer, before adoption of Resolution 281 in 2020, the entirety of Lakeside had never, ever been classified by Talbot County for any sort of development at all — meaning it had never been reviewed with regard to roads and schools and traffic and public safety or its impact on Talbot's rural character.
Like beanfields all over Talbot County, that land was simply designated "unprogrammeed" … not just "the southern 40%." All of it.
But approval of Lakeside was predicated on the falsehood that this unseemly project, no matter how incompatible with our Comprehensive Plan, had been considered and slated for development by Talbot County long, long ago. The developer's point was clear: OK'd earlier, it would be unnecessary and wrong — unfair, in fact — to subject it to another round of review. And so Lakeside got the green light.
THE RECOGNITIONFor over two years, key supporters inside the county continued to back the developer's false claim that the county had slated Lakeside for development in 2002, mocked the very idea that the land had been "unprogrammed," laid out numerous false proofs that the project had been reviewed long ago. After all, the real history was buried away in old documents no one would find, and so the county could get away with accepting as true whatever colorful story the developer wove, no matter how gossamer the thread.
But today both the Maryland Department of the Environment and all of Talbot County know the truth. By "all of Talbot County," I mean the county attorney, the county engineer, the public, members of the Public Works Advisory Board, planning commissioners and County Council members — whether all five acknowledge it publicly or not. The Lakeside land was never approved or even slated for development in years gone by, and in 2020 the developer essentially dodged the legally required review for consistency with our comprehensive plan.
We were conned.
MDE: Last Spring, MDE directed the County to adopt a new Trappe Area Sewer Service Map (the key development document) to correct mistakes made when Lakeside was approved in 2020. MDE confirmed the County's admission that "Map 23" showing Lakeside as UNPROGRAMMED was the proper map, and that reliance on another exhibit ("Map 24") had been a mistake all along. And MDE told the County to correct the mistakes that had been made "including the Lakeside development." In other words, face the truth.
TALBOT COUNTY: The County Engineer wrote MDE last Spring that Map 24 "has created a huge mess," and on numerous occasions since has confirmed that "Map 23," on which all of Lakeside is shown as UNPROGRAMMED, was always the correct Map to use. In responding to the MDE directive, the County Attorney, no doubt with support from elsewhere, seems to The Talbot Integrity Project ("TIP") to have done everything possible to dodge, obfuscate, and avoid the truth and its obvious implication, including drafting legislation that is about as opaque as possible. But finally, eight months after MDE's directive, Mr. Lesher introduced a proposal that compelled the County Attorney to put this simple truth in a recital to Amendment 1 to the Resolution (R348) that is now on the table:
WHEREAS PRIOR TO RESOLUTION 281's ADOPTION BY THE COUNTY COUNCIL AND FINAL APPROVAL BY MDE, FIGURE 23…DEPICTED THE LAKESIDE PARCELS AS "UNPROGRAMMED…"
There you have it. The Emperor stands naked before us. Even the County Attorney, perhaps the key defender of Lakeside, says it's so.
THE TRUTH SHALL SET YOU FREE! Well, maybe.
Given that Talbot County and MDE both acknowledge that the basis for the county's approval of Resolution 281 (and the reason it did not receive a proper review) was, let's say, a "misunderstanding." (in legal parlance, "fraud, surprise, mistake or inadvertence") One might think that mistake would be rectified as fully and directly as possible.
It's simple, really: change the Sewer Service Map to its status before adoption of Resolution 281 to the full extent possible (i.e., but for homes already completed). It's what MDE directed the county to do — fix the mistakes made when adopting the Sewer Service Map in 2020.
Resolution 281 never purported to change the southernmost 40% of Lakeside, and since all of Lakeside was unprogrammed before, that portion remains unprogrammed now. Don't pretend otherwise. And the sewer classification for the rest of Lakeside clearly was changed without proper review, because of "fraud, surprise, mistake or inadvertence" — so change it back, but for the homes already built.
This is the path that about 850 citizens have advocated since last May, having signed the petition still circulating online by the ad hoc Citizens' Committee to Fix Lakeside.
But instead of simplicity we have an opaque mess that pretty much assures that few will fully understand what happened and why until long in the fog has lifted, if ever. It appears at present that a 3-2 majority of the County Council is reluctant or downright unwilling to modify anything that will affect what the developer got out of Resolution 281, con job or not.
That is pretty remarkable.
Three resolutions (R338, R347 and R348) and four separate amendments are on the table so far. They are difficult to follow conceptually and textually. They interconnect and overlap. Depending on what happens to Resolution 348 (and its amendment), Resolution 347 could become moot or require wholesale modification. Map 24 is not eliminated, even though on May 9 MDE requested just that. Important details are buried in a way difficult to see. (e.g., elimination of the "approximately 84" house limit for houses discharging waste into the antiquated Trappe sewer plant).
Formatting is hard to follow. Some recitals are untrue. Resolution 348 purports to limit the Planning Commission's state-granted legal authority even to review the Lakeside property, for "fraud, surprise, mistake or inadvertence," but then Amendment 1 requires the commission to do just that. In a comment to a recent Spy article, a gentleman called it all "word salad". The Star Democrat's reporter Natalie Jones accurately described Mr. Lesher's introduction of the most recent amendment, but after reading the article can you understand how it all fits together?
Stand by for possible further amendments as the council ties itself in knots, trying desperately to pretend even now that the Emperor looks fine.
THE DECISION MAKERSOnly a majority of the County Council can adopt a resolution, but the Planning Commission is the real decision-maker here.
Talbot citizens should recognize that Planning Commissioners and the members of the Public Works Advisory Board (who provide advice on public infrastructure) are in a somewhat awkward spot. Council members are politicians, but members of the Publc Works board and the Planning Commission are not. They want to do what's right on the merits, of course, but no one likes a rocking boat — and no one is anxious for discord with county leadership. Still they have seen the evidence themselves, and now, with MDE's directive and the county's acknowledgement of Lakeside's unprogrammed status pre-Resolution 281, they all surely realize the truth: that in 2020, Resolution 281 was approved only because of the "misunderstandings." Yet it is also clear that some council members (and others they will continue to work with in coming years) are very adamant that Lakeside should not be curtailed in any way.
What to do?
The Planning Commission is the most important link in all this because the commission must first certify any resolution or amendment as "consistent with our Comprehensive Plan" in order for the County Council legally to adopt it. The Public Works Advisory Board advises the commission on infrastructure … and not just water and sewer, but on roads, schools and other public facilities — areas never evaluated in 2020.
The commission and Public Works board are having a joint public work session to review and discuss this whole set of issues at 11 a.m. on Wednesday, Feb. 7, in the Bradley Room at the Courthouse, and the discussion should be of considerable interest.
The Planning Commission does not itself draft or adopt legislation, but they can refuse to find consistent anything that they know is improper, and they can also clarify what a Resolution should include in order to be found consistent with the Comprehensive Plan.
TIP of course is self-aware that over a period of 33 months its advocacy has been not only direct, but sometimes edged towards the strident…which can be counterproductive. That is regretted, but it evolved in the struggle not just to find the truth, but to overcome incomprehensible resistance from some authorities to recognize how the process of approving this billion-dollar deal was corrupted. This is no NIMBY effort, but focuses on the integrity of Talbot County's land use approval process, the character of Talbot County in both senses.
TIP has gone to extraordinary lengths to assure that its claims are backed by actual evidence, hard facts, original documents (e.g., hyperlinks in this letter accessible on the paper's on-line version). Last September TIP delivered to the Planning Commission a letter detailing how Lakeside violates innumerable aspects of the Comprehensive Plan, with a 40-page appendix including transcript excerpts, photos and so forth. That important elucidation of how Lakeside is inconsistent with our Comp Plan has gone unrefuted—in fact, it has not even been discussed, forgotten in all the jockeying about whether the Planning Commission is even authorized to revisit Lakeside issues. TIP also authenticated on-line the whole sordid twenty-year history of Lakeside approvals, and even at this late date remains anxious to meet with any County official, Commissioner, or PWAB member to answer any question that remains.
THE RAMIFICATIONSHaving already acknowledged that prior to Resolution 281 all of Lakeside was actually unprogrammed — so had never before received proper review — the new Sewer Service Map of course should revert to its status before Resolution 281 was adopted (but for land underlying existing houses). The project can be resubmitted in its entirety or in phases, for proper assessment by the Planning Commission when the developer thinks he can demonstrate that it is consistent with our comprehensive plan.
At that point, Talbot County's integrity is restored, proper process in reinstituted, the comp plan honored. Talbot's 37,000 citizens are the beneficiaries. It's what should happen.
Yes, there are plenty of ramifications that fall on the developer. His plans are in disarray. He will have to circle back and actually demonstrate to the Planning Commission for the first time that his development scheme, revised or not, is consistent with the county comp plan. Timing. Schools. Roads and traffic. And yes, even sewerage.
Meanwhile, the developer did get MDE to approve a 100,000-gallon-per-day treatment plant that is under construction. It will serve the homes already built and whatever comes later at Lakeside. The developer's engineer, Rauch, already generated an engineering report on how that plant could treat wastewater in the existing town, which is so much in need of relief. Indeed, in November the town formally adopted that concept as its current policy, and perhaps this turn of events will make the plan even more feasible.
But whatever the repercussions, consider this when balancing the interests of 37,000 Talbot citizens with that of the poor developer: It was the developer's agents who wrongly claimed that Lakeside had been slated for development when in fact it was not. Who never mentioned that Talbot County's only prior review of Lakeside resulted in its rejection 5-0 by the County Council. It was the developer, again through the hard work of his engineer and lawyer, who in 2006 obtained sewer construction permits knowing full well the County had not classified the property "S-1" for immediate development as legally required…and then in 2020 held out those improper permits as evidence that Lakeside had been approved previously.
The developer, Rocks Engineering, has been in the business for years and years and knows the ways of the world. (Two years ago the Washington Post published a link to an archived 1972 article reporting that the development firm's founder had been convicted of federal charges for bribing a Maryland county official regarding zoning.) The real estate business is full of risk. Related to earlier litigation, Mr. Lesher provided an affidavit recounting that when the reversal of R281 was first advanced (back before construction of the first house began), Mr. Showalter acknowledged that his client, Rocks, knew he was proceeding at his own risk regarding a challenge to the legitimacy of R281's approval.
The emperor is naked. Because of a false premise Lakeside was never properly reviewed for consistency with the comprehensive plan. The right thing is to revert the map to the status quo ante, before adoption of Resolution 281, except for homes already built. When the project is resubmitted, as-is or modified, it can then be properly evaluated, including by the Planning Commission for consistency with the comprehensive plan in accordance with statutory standards.
Dan Watson is the acting chair of the Talbot Integrity Project. He lives in Easton.

Dayspring residents face potential eviction amid safety, health concerns

 RIDGELY — For months, residents of the Dayspring Townhomes have raised concerns regarding the safety and conditions of an apartment complex just outside of Ridgely. Now, around half of them are potentially facing eviction.On Nov. 13, the Dayspring Townhomes filed 23 complaints against tenants for failure to pay rent. The complex, located just outside town limits on School Street Lane, is owned by the county and managed by a Delaware-based company.
Failure to pay rent notices were posted to front doors at Daysprings on Friday. A joint trial date for all of the tenants facing eviction is set for this coming Friday afternoon in the Caroline County District Court.
A number of tenants have raised concerns this year about living conditions at the 46-unit complex, including broken appliances, mold, unresponsive property management and an ineffective work order process.
"I've been here 10 years, I ain't never been through this mess," resident Andrea Conaway said on Friday, echoing some of those same concerns.
Those worries only intensified after a non-fatal shooting outside of the complex in August. The incident lead to the county purchasing security cameras, which are now placed at the front of the complex.
Bridge Maryland Inc., a nonprofit organization based in Baltimore County, has held meetings for residents to air their concerns and is assisting the tenants of Dayspring Townhomes with the court process. Bridge Maryland President the Rev. Angelique Mason says residents have experienced the same problems with living conditions for multiple years with no fixes.
"We do know that some of them are not being vocal because they might be behind in their rent," Mason said in an October interview. "They had this idea that they might be evicted if they speak up. And that's really why Bridge is being the voice for the people, because some of them do have fear of eviction. … Nobody should have to live (like that)."
Amid the worries about living conditions, Caroline County paid $2,530 for an independent inspection of the complex on Oct. 23, completed by First State Inspection Agency.
County Administrator Katheleen Freeman said of the 46 units, one was found to have potential mold or mildew. "Outside of that, generally speaking, the most significant issues (were the) smoke detectors," she said in an interview.
The county administrator said East Coast Property Management, the Delaware-based management company that runs the complex, agreed to install the smoke detectors for all units, among other fixes. Attempts by The Star Democrat to reach the company by phone, by email and at their Milford office were unsuccessful.
On Tuesday, Freeman noted that property management informed the county it has addressed electrical issues, fixed broken door frames and ordered window replacements. She said she's expecting other items to be "addressed by the site manager," along with an update next week from East Coast.
The property, which was built in 1994, has been discussed at numerous Caroline County Commissioners meetings since complaints about the apartments surfaced early this year.
On Nov. 12, Commission Vice President Larry Porter expressed his hope that the county sells the property.
"Our position at this point that we're going to express is the possibility of selling that property to a qualified nonprofit organization," Porter said.
In an interview, Porter said the mortgage on the property is deferred because of state involvement, with that deferral conditioned upon the county's ownership and the prerequisite that the property remain a low-income complex.
The complex was previously developed by a nonprofit entity. At last week's commission meeting, Porter said a management agreement between East Coast and the nonprofit — which is no longer in operation — was completed in 2000, and that the language in the agreement needs to be updated.
On Friday evening, some residents in the Dayspring Townhomes had pulled down the notices off of their doors, beginning to process what the future may hold.
Conaway said it was the first time she's received the notice in nearly a decade of living at the complex. Conaway and her daughter, Tiana Corsey, say the living conditions of the 30-year-old townhomes have significantly declined, particularly under the current property manager.
While talking to tenants who had received the notice last week, Bridge Maryland organizer Hannah Freeman said it's time the tenants stand up for themselves, beginning in court this Friday.
"This is why it's important for us to stick together," Hannah Freeman said.

 CAMBRIDGE — A month after a motion to adopt a job description caused tension at a Cambridge City Council meeting, the council unanimously approved the creation of a human resources generalist position for the city.A full-time position, the human resources generalist will assist the city's director of administrative services with daily human resource functions like interviewing staff and resolving departmental issues, according to City Council documents. The salary range for the position is between $73,000 and $83,916.
Before the council's vote at a meeting March 24, Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman said the addition of the position is one step in building the city's Human Resources Department. He said the city will be using consultants to assist in completing a wage study and updating the city's HR manual.
Although the vote to approve the creation of the position was unanimous, the same topic received mixed reviews from city commissioners during a City Council meeting Feb. 24. At that meeting, Commissioner Shay Lewis-Sisco raised concerns with the city's hiring process, and Commissioner Brian Roche said he would like to see evidence of how this position would serve the city's goals.
In February, the motion to adopt a job description for the position — made by Commission President Sputty Cephas — was ultimately voted down.
A month later, before voting to approve the creation of the position, Cambridge commissioners updated residents on their thoughts about the city's request to create the job.
Lewis-Sisco said there was a "lack of clarity" regarding what the council was voting for in February that has since been clarified. She said she understand's the city's vision with its departments.
Roche said he thinks the addition of the human resources generalist position will "build a stronger HR capability," ensure employees are getting the best services and protect the city's interests. He said he would like to see an analysis on where the city is and what is still needed when it comes to human resources.
"Because as a commissioner, I want to know that we have a plan," he said.
Commissioner Frank Stout said he appreciates the thought that went into creating the position. He said he had no objection to moving forward with the resolution.
Commissioner Brett Summers echoed Stout's comments, adding he thinks the minimum job qualifications for the position could be increased.
Currently, the job description requires that applicants hold a bachelor's degree in human resources, business administration or a related field and become HIPAA certified within two weeks of being hired. The description states at least one year of human resource management experience is preferred.
At the end of the discussion, Cephas thanked Steckman for acknowledging a need in a city department and bringing it to the council.
"The motion is to approve the creation of the position," Cephas said for clarity. "We're not approving to hire anybody."

 EASTON — Candidates for Town Council president are speaking out against recent sign vandalism ahead of Easton's May 6 election.In a letter to police Thursday, current President Frank Gunsallus said he was notified that a swastika was placed on one of his campaign signs at the corner of South Aurora Street and South Lane. He said that came after "significant vandalism" of a number of his other signs.
"This act of hate has escalated the situation into a deeply troubling reality that demands our collective attention," Gunsallus wrote.
Don Abbatiello, the current Ward 2 representative running against Gunsallus for the presidential seat, said theft and vandalism do not belong in the town's elections.
In an interview Friday, Abbatiello said he informed Gunsallus of the defaced sign after discovering it while campaigning in town Wednesday.
"We obviously disagree on some issues, we're running against each other, but there's no reason to deface people's property," Abbatiello said. "There's no reason to bring hatred into this at all. We are still a community. We're still neighbors. We should act like it."
Gunsallus contacted the Easton Police Department after seeing the South Aurora Street sign. He also says campaign signs have been stolen from his home.
Abbatiello says a few of his signs have gone missing as well, though he's unsure if they were stolen or blew away due to wind.
Interim Town Manager Alan Lowrey, Easton's police chief, said an investigation into the defaced sign on South Aurora Street is underway. Lowrey told The Star Democrat that as for missing signs, some were taken down by town code enforcers due to violating town code.
Political sign violations include too many signs on one property or signs placed in a public right-of-way, Lowrey said. To avoid confusion moving forward, Lowrey has asked code enforcement to notify him of any signs not within the code so he can contact the candidate.
Lowrey says he's reached out to both Abbatiello and Gunsallus regarding signs that need to be moved or removed due to town code. Both candidates have complied, Lowrey noted.
Gunsallus and Abbatiello each denounced sign vandalism and acts of hatred.
"These types of things shouldn't happen during a campaign," Gunsallus wrote in a statement to The Star Democrat. "However, I'm hopeful this can be a turning point for our town to come together, reject hate, and foster love in its place."
"We're a community, we all live here together," Abbatiello said. "We need to get along with one another. And bringing in things like that, totally uncalled for."
Easton Police Department Sgt. Patrick Sally says stealing or defacing political signs are criminal offenses. He emphasized that many homeowners and businesses have security technology, such as Ring cameras, that can help identify those stealing or defacing signs.

Crimes relating to fraud of older residents are likely the biggest financial loss in the county, he added.Gamble identified juvenile crimes in schools as a particular issue for the sheriff's office, which has uniformed officers serving in most of the public schools.Recently implemented state juvenile justice reform laws have barred police from charging anyone under 13 with most crimes.Gamble said Easton High School and Easton Middle School are where police see most of the incidents involving children, and over 30% of this year's reported incidents involve children under 13."We have 12-year-olds that are punching other kids in the face time and time again in the schools, or assaulting other kids, and there's no services for them," he said.Police Accountability Board members acknowledged the concerns, asking what officers can do to better handle issues with youth under 13 and if police can work with the schools.Gamble said the school system doesn't have leverage to handle discipline other than resorting to suspensions.Looking forward, Gamble hopes to see movement within state leadership in Annapolis during the upcoming General Assembly session to push legislation to tackle issues with the juvenile reform laws.Outside of juvenile crime, those at the meeting discussed several recent local incidents.In Easton, two homicides occurred within town limits in the last few months - one on Blake Street in early August and a second at the Sidetracked Saloon in late September.Several thefts and robberies have also occurred in town, said Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey. It's just going to be a little while," he said.Oxford Police Chief Eric Kellner did not report any major issues, adding that Oxford is a "very safe little town." The town is now looking to hire one additional officer.

 Two teens allegedly attempted to carjack a man at gunpoint at an Elkton carwash — a crime that was captured on video by a business security camera, according to the Elkton Police Department.Investigators identified the suspects as Landon Shane Diebold and Aiden Anthony Meadows, both of whom are 18 and both of whom are Elkton residents who reside at the same address.
The investigation leading to their arrests and the charges against them started at approximately 3 a.m. on Friday, when EPD officers rushed to the Elkton Car Wash in the 500 block of North Bridge Street after receiving a dispatch regarding an attempted armed robbery, police reported.
According to Cecil County District Court records, the victim told investigators that three males dressed in all-black clothing approached him on foot as he was seated in his car a short distance outside Bay 3, where he was cleaning his interior windshield.
The video, which lacks audio, shows one of the masked suspects pulling a handgun out of a tan bag that is on his waist and then pointing the weapon at the victim for a few seconds, before putting the firearm back into the pouch and running away, court records indicate.
Police reported that the victim told investigators that he did not respond to the threat made at gunpoint and that his resistance caused the suspects to flee.
In addition to the all-black clothing, two of the suspects wore ski masks to conceal their facial features, police said. The third — later identified as Meadows — was not wearing a ski mask, and that helped EPD investigators identify him, court records show.
"While walking away from the (victim) and nearer to the camera, the unmasked male with long brown curly hair is clearly identifiable as Aiden Meadows," according to the charging document.
The lead investigator, EPD Detective J. Jollie, notes in his written statement of probable cause that he is familiar with Meadows because of his "prior encounters and interactions" with him during his law enforcement career, court records show.
In that court document, Jollie also reports that he is familiar with Diebold.
"I am familiar with Aiden and his associates because of prior investigations regarding the theft of firearms and the theft of vehicles. One of the associates Aiden is known to commit these types of crimes with in the past is Landon Diebold. Diebold has a thin build and tall frame, similar to that of the perpetrator in the video that retrieves, displays and points the firearm toward (the victim)," court records allege.
In addition, according to the charging document, Diebold's distinctive tattoos, which could be seen on the security-camera footage, helped investigators identify him as a suspect — despite him wearing a ski mask.
"Diebold has tattoos on his hands. I then accessed Diebold's Instagram account . . . and reviewed his profile picture. Within this picture, Diebold's hand tattoos are visible and tattooed on his left hand is red lettering, directly next to a dark arch, which also is close in proximity to a dark round figure," Jollie explains in the written charging document.
EPD officers and detectives worked throughout the better part of Friday to identify, locate and arrest Diebold and Meadows, according to police. During a court-approved search, investigators found and confiscated two guns, police reported.
As of Tuesday, investigators still were trying to identify the third suspect. Anyone with information that might help in this investigation is asked to email EPD Detective Jollie at jjollie@elktonpd.org. EPD officials posted a press release about the alleged attempted carjacking on the agency's Facebook page on Monday morning, along with mugshots of Diebold and Meadows.
Diebold is facing 11 criminal charges, including first-degree assault, armed robbery, use of a handgun in the commission of a felony or a crime of violence, handgun on person and attempted carjacking, according to Cecil County District Court records.
Meadows is facing 10 criminal charges — all of them the same as those filed against Diebold, court records show. Meadows, however, is not charged with handgun on person — the additional charge that Diebold is facing, according to court records.
Both remained in the Cecil County Detention Center on no bond Tuesday, one day after their bail review hearings in front of Cecil County District Court Judge Clara E. Campbell, court records show.

title: From signs to survival: a family’s kidney campaign
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
From signs to survival: a family’s kidney campaign

 August 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 883

 POTOMAC, Md. — Melanie Flamenbaum and her family are on a life-saving mission to find kidney donors for her sister and brother-in-law, Dana and Andrew Goldstein of Lewes, Del.Her husband, Ed Goldstein, and their sons, Ranan and Brooks, have been posting signs linking to the National Kidney Registry website. They've placed the signs in storefront windows, near a soybean field at the Inn at Huntingfield Creek, and even at a Boston Red Sox–Washington Nationals game.
Last weekend, they brought the campaign to Kent County while picking up Brooks from camp at Echo Hill. The family stayed in Rock Hall, enjoying the peaceful surroundings while continuing to spread awareness.
Throughout High Street in Chestertown and surrounding areas, signs share information about Dana and Andrew's circumstances and promote awareness of organ donation.
Flamenbaum said she overcame any shyness to give her sister and brother-in-law a chance to live and witness future milestones — including those of their daughter, Jelena Goldstein, who recently earned a master's degree from the University of Delaware.
Dana and Andrew's story is deeply personal and heart-wrenching.
Both in their 50s, Dana and Andrew have lived with Type 1 diabetes most of their lives, Flamenbaum told Kent County News.
Andrew was diagnosed in infancy. He underwent radiation treatments that left him with one functioning kidney and a pancreas that never fully recovered.
Dana was diagnosed at age 8 and has been taking insulin ever since.
Originally from New York, the couple met while attending Case Western Reserve University in Ohio. Andrew studied biomedical engineering, and they bonded over their shared experiences managing diabetes. They fell in love, got married and later welcomed Jelena.
Despite their medical challenges, the couple thrived for years. Andrew built a career in the biomedical field, and Dana held various jobs before focusing on raising their daughter.
But toward the end of the COVID-19 pandemic, their lives changed dramatically.
Dana was rushed to the emergency room with breathing difficulties and tested positive for COVID-19. She spent two weeks on a ventilator in the ICU and faced a long recovery once discharged.
Even after the couple relocated to Lewes in 2022, Dana continued to struggle. Climbing stairs became difficult, and weakness persisted. At a routine checkup, her blood and kidney levels raised concern. Soon after, she began dialysis treatment.
Dana initially underwent hemodialysis three days a week, where blood is drained through a chest port, cleaned, and returned to the body. The process was exhausting and consumed much of her energy.
Eventually, she transitioned to peritoneal dialysis at home. Using a port in her abdomen, a cleansing solution flows into the body and is later drained through a hose into the shower. While more convenient than hospital visits, the daily process was just as draining. At first, she performed treatments four times a day. Now, she undergoes dialysis overnight for eight hours while sleeping.
Andrew was by her side through it all, specially trained to help administer treatment. But soon, his own health began to decline.
After attending a social event, Andrew contracted pneumonia and began experiencing kidney failure. Like his wife, he started with hemodialysis and now performs peritoneal dialysis at home.
Flamenbaum said that while he is still able to work from home, it is not sustainable long term.
"Diabetes and dialysis have taken over their life," she said.
Everyday tasks have become increasingly difficult. Boxes of dialysis solution are stacked in the living room — a constant reminder of their new reality.
"Activities we take for granted, like a routine trip for a cup of coffee, are a draining affair for them," Flamenbaum said. "It takes a force of will to just do something natural."
That's why the family is being proactive — raising awareness, reaching out to as many people as possible, and dispelling fears and misconceptions about kidney donation.
With her loved ones' lives on the line, Flamenbaum has become well-versed in the process.
She explained that through the National Kidney Registry's voucher program, finding a compatible donor is now easier and more efficient than ever. Donors undergo a comprehensive medical exam, speak with doctors and counselors, and can opt out at any time with no pressure.
While kidney donation is still a major procedure, Flamenbaum said it is one of the safest surgeries with a relatively short recovery time.
"Someone who receives an organ from a live donor can generally go back to work immediately," she said — something Dana and Andrew hope to be able to do again.
Receiving a kidney from a living donor also means a lower chance of rejection, fewer anti-rejection medications, and fewer long-term complications.
For donors, she said the risk is minimal.
"I've talked to people who have donated," she said. "One told me, 'If not for a small scar, I wouldn't even know I did this.'"
But the emotional and spiritual reward, she said, is immense.
"They feel really good, emotionally and spiritually, because they've given someone their quality of life back," Flamenbaum said.
That's the outcome Dana and Andrew are fighting for as they continue their campaign across Maryland and surrounding states. If successful, they plan to have their transplant surgeries at the MedStar Georgetown Transplant Institute, one of the country's highest-volume organ transplant programs.
For more information or to begin the donor screening process, visit: nkr.org/TDE863 for Dana or nkr.org/TKZ944 for Andrew.
"We want to spread our message as broadly as possible," Flamenbaum said. "We take our signs everywhere we go — and we're not stopping."

Cambridge City Council hears plans for Harriet Tubman mural area

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge mayor and commissioners spent a significant portion of their three-hour meeting Monday learning about Alpha Genesis Community Development Corporation's plans to revitalize the area surrounding the Harriet Tubman mural behind 424 Race St.Adrian Holmes, president and program director of Alpha Genesis, said the second phase project will help extend the stay of tourists in Cambridge.
"Right now, most people who go back there stay no longer than five or ten minutes because there's nowhere to sit, it's hot, it's just not really appealing," she said. "So this is what we want to do to help the people who come to the mural extend their stay. And when they extend their stay, they'll spend more money ... and they'll just have a better experience."
The plan, which extends into Cannery Way off Race Street, is to add two retail spaces adjacent the mural. One of the spaces will be a souvenir shop, Holmes said. The building itself will also include Alpha Genesis' headquarters, three other retail spaces that face Race Street and an exhibition deck.
In front of the mural will be the Harriet Tubman Pavilion, which will shield viewers from inclement weather. Near the pavilion, there will be a community garden.
"We affectionately call this project the North Star Village, a tribute in honor of Harriet Tubman," Holmes said.
Alpha Genesis has been working with the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development, the Maryland Historical Trust, the Rural Maryland Council, state legislators and the City of Cambridge to make enhancements to the space. Alpha Genesis is still raising funds for the second phase of the project, which will cost around $1.5 million. The project has received funding from the Maryland General Assembly and the city.
"And then we have a couple grant opportunities that can cover the rest of it," Holmes said.
According to council meeting documents, the proximity of Alpha Genesis' property to city property has made the project a "joint venture" between the two. One document from Alpha Genesis states the city will improve Cannery Way and the adjacent parking lot, and Alpha Genesis will focus on 428 through 432 Race St.
Alpha Genesis is asking the city for the installation of public restrooms, the repositioning of the brick wall on Cannery Way and the addition of a replica of the Ben Ross Cabin on the Cannery Way property.
Holmes said restrooms would benefit tourists who come from far distances to see the mural. Alpha Genesis' proposal is to construct a "North Star Station" that includes two all-gender bathrooms, a 135-square-foot public meeting room and a small lobby space with digital kiosks that have information about the city.
RESTROOM DISCUSSIONCommissioners asked a variety of questions about Alpha Genesis' plans. Multiple questions focused on the restroom proposal.
Commissioner Brian Roche shared his concern with the North Star Station blocking the view of the water from Cannery Way. Holmes said a possible change to the proposal could be to remove the meeting room from the station to make it smaller.
Commission President Sputty Cephas asked who would be responsible for maintaining the public restrooms. Alpha Genesis Executive Director Jermaine Anderson said he thinks it would be a good idea to form a youth or recidivism program where those in the program would be tasked with maintaining areas around the mural.
"Now's the time," he said. "Let's get real creative. Let's continue planning, continue talking, developing relationships. ... I think we can find the solutions we need."
During public comment, Chuck McFadden said he supports revitalizing the area, but the city should be careful about how much it commits. McFadden also cautioned that bringing youth in to clean the public restrooms might not be an easy feat.
After council discussion, the City Council unanimously voted to have city staff work closely with Alpha Genesis on its proposal and make sure it gets through the Historic Preservation Commission and the Planning and Zoning Commission. The vote, which Cephas motioned, also called for a presentation on the fiscal impact of the proposal and made sure Roche and any other interested commissioners can work with city staff on the matter.
