title: ICE outlines immigration enforcement as QA officials explore 287(g) agreement
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN and HANNAH COMBS
content:
ICE outlines immigration enforcement as QA officials explore 287(g) agreement

 August 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN and HANNAH COMBS | Section: Local News 
 
 790
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — As Queen Anne's County leaders weigh the possibility of entering a formal partnership with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, community members and officials remain divided.U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Agent James Brooks spoke to a full room July 30 during a Queen Anne's County Republican Central Committee informational session, offering a nonpartisan overview of ICE's operations, national enforcement protocols and local implications.
Brooks, the community relations officer for ICE's Washington and Baltimore field offices, outlined the agency's primary focus on enforcing immigration law as enacted by Congress. ICE is tasked with identifying, arresting, detaining and removing individuals unlawfully present in the United States.
Underscoring the complexity of the issue at hand after decades of interpretation and practice by several White House administrations. "Immigration law is the second most complex set of codes next to tax codes," Brooks said.
reviewing options
In separate interviews, Queen Anne's County Commissioner Chris Corchiarino and Sheriff Gary Hofmann said the county's intent is to "fully comply" with federal mandates. They noted that many components of the 287(g) program — through which local jurisdictions partner with ICE on immigration enforcement — are already being fulfilled within the scope of current capabilities.
For example, there is a designated desk for ICE agents at the county sheriff's office, and at least one recent transfer has been made from the county detention center to immigration officials, officials said.
In July, county leadership assembled a task force to study the 287(g) program. The group — composed of Corchiarino, Hofmann, legal counsel and a representative from the detention center — is evaluating the purpose of such an agreement, the potential fiscal impact and any legal liabilities.
Corchiarino said the county commissioners would be required to vote before entering into any agreement. That vote could take place as early as this fall. He added that any needed funding could be drawn from the existing budget.
"As a sheriff, my commitment is to foster a safe environment for all members of our community, regardless of their citizenship status," Hofmann said. "We recognize the complexities of immigration laws and the impact they can have on federal funding. Our priority is to protect our citizens from gangs, criminals and violent offenders while also showing compassion and support for our immigrant community."
Understanding ICE operations
Brooks explained that ICE's operational components include Enforcement and Removal Operations, which conducts arrests and removals, and Homeland Security Investigations, which investigates transnational crimes.
"We don't go out and see who we can arrest," Brooks said. "We already know who we are targeting when ICE is going out to effect arrests."
He stressed that ICE detention is meant to streamline the deportation process, not to punish.
However, due to Maryland's "Dignity Not Detention" law, ICE must seek out-of-state facilities for detainees, oftentimes in Pennsylvania or Virginia.
Maryland has no ICE detention centers, only field holding offices — meaning the Baltimore and Salisbury centers for ICE do not contain beds and are not designed to house detainees past a temporary hold. The goal aims to transfer individuals "within hours," Brooks said. But he could not confirm what current protocol and practices are at those offices.
At press time, ICE had not responded to follow-up inquiries about these procedures.
The removal process, he noted, is far more involved than simply returning an immigrant to their country of origin. It often includes considerations for asylum, travel documentation, legal proceedings before an immigration judge, and agreements with third-party countries.
Brooks said while ICE officers often face criticism, morale remains high within the Baltimore field office. "Officers are busy but good. They know they're making a difference in their communities by going after the worst of the worst," he said.
He added that some officers choose to wear masks when in public as a personal safety measure due to the agency's current public image.
Community perspectives
The presentation was meant to provide factual, nonpartisan information, according to QACRCC President Helen Bennett.
"I think it counter-balances the misinformation that is out there," Bennett said. "And really, knowledge is power and we need to get information that is real, viable and truthful."
Bennett said she was particularly surprised to learn about the lack of ICE detention centers in Maryland, calling out-of-state transfers "a pretty penny." She noted that many attendees expressed interest in learning more about forming a 287(g) agreement.
Committee member Rick Bowers voiced his personal belief that the county should "fully engage" with ICE to enhance public safety and federal resource access.
Conversely, Queen Anne's County Democratic Central Committee Chair Elaine McNeil said her committee opposes entering into a 287(g) agreement.
"They just want a new start. And we're all trying to enjoy that ourselves," McNeil said of immigrants. She expressed concern that individuals could be "unlawfully processed and treated in a manner like some kind of criminal."
The topic remains under discussion by the Democratic committee, she said.

title: Demolition of remaining Key Bridge structures beginning around July 7

Demolition of remaining Key Bridge structures beginning around July 7

 Demolition of the remaining Key Bridge structures will begin on or about July 7, the Maryland Transportation Authority announced on June 26.The work is expected to take several months to complete and will involve the use of heavy machinery to dismantle what is left of the bridge.
The process will begin with the removal of the bridge deck over the river, followed by demolition of sections over Hawkins Point and then Sollers Point, the Maryland Transportation Authority said in a release.
This phase of work focuses on removing portions of the existing structure that interfere with the alignment of the new bridge.
No controlled detonations will occur.
The general demolition sequence will include the removal of deck, barriers and parapets over the river from both Hawkins Point and Sollers Point, followed by the removal of deck, barriers, parapets, girders and piers on the landside approaches, down to just below ground level.
Finally, the original north and south abutments will be removed.
Nearby communities should expect to see active tug and barge operations on the river, with heavy equipment and trucks visible on the existing bridge structure.
Barges will serve as protective shielding during demolition and must be avoided by waterway users. Machinery used may include excavators, concrete saws, vacuums, cranes and trucks.
An on-site concrete crusher will recycle materials for haul roads and staging areas, reducing truck trips and cost.
Typical large construction project noise is expected from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.
Equipment is being installed in nearby communities to capture baseline noise and vibration data before the start of demolition and upcoming construction activities.
Buoys will mark a safety zone, no entry area around active work areas.
Notices will be issued to designate speed restrictions and safety zones to ensure the safe passage of vessels near the construction area.
The Maryland Transportation Authority said that it will continue to provide updates and advance notice of any work that may affect nearby communities, roads or waterways.
Based on months of field investigations and engineering analysis, the bridge alignment is slightly east or downriver of the original structure, remaining entirely within the Maryland Transportation Authority's existing right-of-way. To proceed with construction, the Maryland Transportation Authority is requesting modifications to permits that have been issued by the Maryland Board of Public Works, Maryland Department of the Environment, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the U.S. Coast Guard in support of the Key Bridge Rebuild, according to the release.
The permit modification requests will reflect updates to the bridge pier foundation design, pier protection elements, and trestle configuration. They also include a decrease in authorized impacts to tidal waters and some additional impacts to non-tidal wetlands and waterways.
A reevaluation of the project's categorical exclusion will also be submitted to the Federal Highway Administration.
No significant increase in environmental impacts is expected, the release said.

title: What they do doesn't always match what they say
author: DAVID REEL
content:
What they do doesn't always match what they say

 July 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns

 Read News Document

 Following Richard Nixon's election as president in 1968, John Mitchell, Nixon's campaign manager, was asked by the media what to expect when Nixon assumed office.Mitchell said prophetically long before Watergate, "Watch what we do, not what we say."
Those words apply to many candidates for public office today.
The are at least two recent examples in Maryland.
Prior to leaving office after two terms, Republican Gov. Larry Hogan proclaimed he had no interest in running for an open U.S. Senate seat in Maryland formerly held by Ben Cardin.
Hogan went as far as saying his experience as a business executive and eight years serving as governor, left him reluctant to serve in a deeply divided legislative body marked by lengthy and often bitterly partisan dialogue and decision making.
Then in February 2024 Hogan entered the Senate race where he easily won the Republican nomination in a primary election but lost in the general election with 42.8% of votes cast.
In 2022, Wes Moore was elected as Hogan's Democratic successor with 64.5% of votes cast.
Almost immediately following his election Moore was widely viewed by political pundits in Maryland, Washington, D.C., and nationally as a potential presidential candidate in 2028.
To date, Moore has said early and often regularly he is not pursuing that goal.
Despite saying that, it has been most interesting watching media reports of what Moore has done in the political arena during his first term as governor.
Moore ...
Spoke at the 2024 Democratic National Convention.Campaigned for Kamala Harris in Pennsylvania, North Carolina and Michigan.Campaigned for Democratic candidates in Virginia.Appeared on The View where Joyce Behar told him he looked "very presidential."Interviewed with CNN following his college commencement speech in southeastern Pennsylvania.Attended an Aspen Colorado fundraiser hosted by Damian O'Doherty, a Maryland political operative and co-founder of Baltimore based KO Public Affairs.Shared his thoughts on "bold, purposeful leadership" on a podcast with the NBA's Golden State Warriors head coach Steve Kerr and CBS Evening News co-anchor John Dickerson.Delivered a keynote speech at the South Carolina Democratic Blue Palmetto Dinner.Attended a fish fry hosted by Congressman Jim Clyburn who is widely credited for a Joe Biden 2020 primary campaign resurgence when that campaign was stalled.Met with former political advisers to Barack Obama and Joe Biden to discuss a presidential path to the White House through South Carolina.Spoke to hundreds of political insiders in South Carolina about his personal biography and on his record as Maryland governor.Spoke at an NAACP "Fight for Freedom" dinner in Detroit, Michigan.Spoke at the Virginia Democratic Party's Blue Commonwealth Gala.Will attend The Sun Valley Conference in Idaho sponsored by private investment firm Allen & Company, which is branded by Fortune magazine as an annual "billionaire summer camp," that brings together business executives, social media titans, traditional news figures and elected officials who aspire to become president.
Ultimately, all this travel and schmoozing by Moore may be for naught.
Next year, Moore must win a Democratic primary election and a general election in Maryland.
Conventional wisdom that he will win both is far from a given.
In polling done earlier this year, Moore's job performance approval fell to 55% from 61% from polling done in the prior month.
These poll results occurred before Moore signed into law a wide range of tax increases, new taxes, fee increases and new fees that were approved in the 2025 general assembly session.
As I write this, Moore has an opponent in the 2026 Democratic primary and three potential opponents seeking a gubernatorial nomination in the 2026 Republican primary. He will have a Green Party candidate in the 2026 general election.
In the Democratic and Republican primaries there may be more candidates deciding to run.
One wild card in the Republican primary is former Governor Hogan.
Despite his failed U.S. Senate run, a survey done after Hogan's two terms as governor, showed he had a 77% job approval rating that included an 81% approval rating with Democratic voters.
Hogan has not yet announced his decision on seeking a third term which the state constitution allows since it would not be a third successive term.
Assuming Moore is the successful Democratic candidate for governor, there is also the hard political reality that not meeting expected vote totals in elections that any candidate is expected to win can be an insurmountable roadblock on a journey to the White House.
Preeminent Maryland political analyst Len Foxwell has observed: "What we have seen in the past where prospective gubernatorial candidates and prospective presidential candidates have been derailed because of weaker than expected showings back home."
Regardless of who is elected Maryland governor in 2026, voters in that election cycle and every election cycle in Maryland would be best served if there was no longer a regular mismatch between what some candidates of every party affiliation do and what they say.

 September 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News

 A new display outside of city hall ensures that prisoners of war and service members still missing in action will never be forgotten in Newark, Delaware.The Newark Morning Rotary Club unveiled a POW/MIA Chair of Honor during a brief ceremony Thursday evening, on the eve of National POW/MIA Recognition Day.
"The Chair of Honor will surely stand as a testament to our commitment to remembering and respecting the courage and dedication of the brave individuals who we honor today," club president Jamie Zingaro said. "It also reminds us of the horrors of war and the tremendous impact war has on our families. As Rotarians, we recognize the importance of service above self, and this memorial will continue to remind us of the service and sacrifices so many have made to keep us free."
Hundreds of POW/MIA Chairs of Honor can be found in public spaces around the country, ranging from professional sports stadiums to city halls, and even the U.S. Capitol Building. The perpetually empty chair is meant to help people remember that even though the soldiers are not here, there's always a place for them.
Newark already has a Chair of Honor that is used at the annual Memorial Day ceremony and displayed inside city hall. However, the new one is suitable for outdoor display.
The chair was installed in an area of the city hall parking lot that also includes flagpoles and a plaque honoring city employees who served in the military. It is surrounded by stanchions topped with symbols representing each of the branches of the military, and a bronze plaque explains the purpose of the chair and includes the words "You are not forgotten."
With the blessing of city council, the Rotary Club funded the project and committed to maintaining the display in the future.
Rosely Robinson, who has helped install dozens of Chairs of Honor throughout Delaware and surrounding states, noted that since World War II, there are still 81,000 service members unaccounted for.
"Outside of their families and friends, they have nearly been forgotten," Robinson said. "This chair serves as a constant reminder of those still missing and that we have a place for them when they come home."
Of those missing, 121 are from Delaware.
"It doesn't sound like a big number, but 121 families, brothers, sisters, moms and dads are still waiting, and they should never be forgotten," Robinson said.
Ralph Galati, an Air Force captain whose plane was shot down over North Vietnam, was a prisoner of war for 14 months.
"It was not heroic. It was not brave," Galati said. "But it was performing one's duty, hopefully with dignity and to be able to return with honor."
He said he and his fellow prisoners showed their resolve through resistance by having church services, singing the national anthem and reciting the Pledge of Allegiance.
"All of them were forbidden to be discussed and performed during captivity," he said. "Yet they were the very things that mattered the most to us, so we proudly recited them, regardless of the punishment or consequences. And today, none of these are taken lightly by me. It could be a flag flying gently overhead, or a song before a baseball game or a great rendition of the national anthem, the impact is still the same."

 According to state Board of Elections, Instructions and Information for Challengers, Watchers, and Other Election Observers, reissued Oct. 14, 2022, Part III, Item 19 answers the question: "Can a polling place open if the election judges represent only one political party?" "Yes." Under advice from the attorney general, the election judges present must open the polling place by the required time, even if there are election judges of only one political party present.As an election judge who has served in the past, I am honored to execute this civic service with my fellow judges, regardless of their affiliation.
First-time judges are often humbled and impressed by the security, objectivity, support and training mandated and effected by both the state and county Boards of Elections.
Talbot County's director of elections has repeatedly made it known that there is an imbalance of affiliation and has encouraged recruitment of Republican applicants.
For staffing purposes, the board must have a commitment from anyone wishing to serve well in advance of the election. I think the board contacted judges who had participated in 2022 as early as October 2023 to inquire about interest in serving for the 2024 cycle.
It is a long game. Not quite as long as the campaigns, thankfully.
Judges report to their assigned polling places by 5:45 a.m. and must stay until all eligible voters have voted, the equipment is secured and the chief judge is ready to take the results to the board office. Everyone leaves as a group. It is a long day. The board must also staff and support early voting (Oct. 24-31).
Please make your plan to vote and do so with faith and trust that election staff and judges want to provide an objective environment to cast your ballot.

title: Easton approves restrictions on campaign donations
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton approves restrictions on campaign donations

 October 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News

 EASTON — Candidates in future campaigns will face new fundraising restrictions and reporting requirements thanks to a new law passed by the Easton Town Council.After nearly six months of fine-tuning, Easton passed its first campaign finance ordinance on Monday.
It will limit campaign contributions to $1,000, ban contributions from political committees and organizations, and require campaign treasurers to submit detailed financial reports before and after the election.
Council members said the ordinance is a win for transparency in Easton's elections. All five voted in favor of the new regulations.
"I think that (we) have done an excellent job of putting together an ordinance which achieves our goals of providing transparency in elections," said Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery, who sponsored the ordinance alongside Mayor Megan Cook.
The ordinance was introduced in April, amid a heated and politically charged race between current Town Council President Don Abbatiello and former President Frank Gunsallus.
There were largely no requirements for candidates to report specific contributions made to their campaigns during this year's election. Financial disclosures submitted by candidates when they filed for candidacy didn't include campaign donations. Montgomery, Cook and others argued that there should be more transparency on which organizations and people make donations to candidates.
Now, future candidates must name a campaign treasurer, who is responsible for sending the town office documentation of each donation, whether from an individual, business or organization.
The council has made several edits to the campaign ordinance ordinance since April, including raising the maximum donation mark from $250 to $1,000 and exempting spouses or domestic partners of candidates from the $1,000 limit.
Ward 2 Councilmember Robert Rankin said Monday that concerns he had about a political committee donation ban in the ordinance breaching First Amendment standards were quelled after discussion with Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh.
Rankin said individuals involved in political organization can still donate on behalf of themselves. And the ordinance doesn't stop political committees from making "independent expenditures" supporting a candidate, as long as the money doesn't go to the candidate directly.
Political groups will be required to file reports to the town if their expenses for an election cycle are $100 or more.
Town elections are nonpartisan.
Resident Lance Simon, a vocal advocate for the ordinance, thanked council members for supporting the new restrictions and said he hopes it can be "up and running" soon to allow enough time for it to be properly implemented. The town's next election is scheduled for May 2027.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis, who expressed concerns with the first draft of the ordinance potentially blocking some residents from running for office due to fiscal limits, said Monday that the final version is in a better place.
Davis thanked Cook and Montgomery for sponsoring the ordinance and bringing transparency to future town elections.
"I think the work has been done," Davis said. "I think we have really mulled it over a lot."

title: Long-awaited Easton dog park officially opens

Long-awaited Easton dog park officially opens

 January 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News

 EASTON — Not even sub-freezing temperatures and bits of ice laying on the turf grass Thursday morning could stop over a dozen dogs — and their owners — from celebrating the grand opening of Easton's long-awaited dog park.Dogs of all ages, sizes and breeds were pulling at their leashes with energetic anticipation, waiting for the ceremonial red ribbon to be cut by Easton Mayor Megan Cook.
Thursday's ribbon cutting was a welcome sight for local dog owners and dog lovers, many of whom had waited years for the project to come to fruition.
A voiced interest in a dog park first came seven or eight years ago, said Rick Van Emburgh, the town engineer.
But in 2019, Easton residents David Ferraris and Noah Matten restarted the efforts, working with Rauch Inc., a local engineering firm, to prepare concept plans for a dog park near the downtown area.
And in fall 2020, the town received $7 million in bond funding, a majority of which was required to be allocated to parks.
Almost three years later, in March 2023, the Easton Town Council voted to fully fund the dog park on Brewers Lane and to add a restroom there, Van Emburgh said.
With the legislative work completed, construction of the dog park required a true group effort from the town's public works, parks and recreation, IT, buildings and finance departments.
Willow Construction, Easton Utilities and Chester River Landscaping also lent a hand with a number of other efforts to make the park a reality.
"I believe this is a wonderful example of teamwork," Van Emburgh said. "I believe it's a wonderful example of our community working together to build something beautiful for our town residents and our dogs."
Cook kept her comments brief, acknowledging a number of excitedly yapping dogs waiting to enter the park and play.
"I really want to give an extra shoutout to all the departments," the mayor said. "Pretty much every department in the Town of Easton played a role in getting this park up and running."
Once the ribbon was cut, the dogs were unleashed and off to play.
The new park, open dawn to dusk, includes two separate play areas for the pups based on weight, with a larger area allocated to dogs over 35 pounds.
A turf grass layer on top makes for a comfortable surface for dogs to run, jump and roll around, and underneath, there's an anti-microbial infill material and an irrigation system for cooling the turf.
It was clear that the dogs were excited as they raced in circles and made new friends, and the smiles on owners' faces told a similar story.
Easton resident Scott Cohen, who stopped by the park with his two Australian Shepherd-poodle mixes Scruffy, 4, and Casey, 3, said the dogs had a great time playing Thursday morning.
"I think it's a terrific add to the community," he said.

The Smiths tried everything, from medication to a month-long rehabilitation program to natural supplements. Stacey Smith said none of it worked.

title: Commissioners of Oxford hear plans for portable pump stations

Commissioners of Oxford hear plans for portable pump stations

 OXFORD — In an effort to address flooding caused by rainy day events, Oxford is looking into setting up portable stormwater pump stations across town.During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, engineer Wayne Newton presented plans to install four temporary, portable pump stations in three locations in town: Two stations near the causeway, one station at Bank Street and one station at Mill Street.
Newton is the president of Messick & Associates, an engineering firm the town has a contract with. He said he expects the pump stations will relieve moderate flooding, which he defined as anything less than storm surge.
"A storm surge comes in, it comes over the bulkhead, it comes over the causeway, that's not what we're planning for here," he said. "We're just planning for rainy day events."
Oxford Wastewater Superintendent Matt Ozman, who has been working closely with Newton, said the pumps will allow the town to drain water faster.
"It's the plan of moving the water where it's not going to take us days, it'll be hours," Ozman said.
Oxford Commission President Norm Bell said the town is trying to take a step back, look at what it would like to see in the future and determine what is needed today in order to build toward that.
"So this is more of a holistic viewpoint than what we've been looking at previously," he said.
Commissioner Tom Costigan said the portable pump stations are more flexible than permanent pump stations in the ground.
"You can take our solution and move it to where the problem is instead of having a problem and saying, 'Oh, well we've got this really neat pump station eight blocks away,'" he said.
Along with placing portable pump stations in the low-lying areas Newton identified, Newton also outlined plans to address the existing drain system on Mill Street that runs through the marina. He said he would like to re-grade and rebuild some of the drain system so water drains toward the water tower and the pump station can be moved to that area.
"We'd prefer (the pump station) to be down there," Newton said about the area where the water tower is. "There's more room for it down there."
Newton said over the next month, his office plans to work on designs and cost estimates for the project that he can bring back to the commissioners for review. He said his goal is to have the project complete by the end of 2025.
The project will be funded using American Rescue Plan Act funds.
Ozman considers this project to be laying the foundation when it comes to addressing flooding issues. He said the town can hone in on these three areas first, then address flooding in other areas.
"We're trying to do the best that we can with the money that's available at the time without having to spend millions on something that can't be moved, can't be touched, can't be retrofitted," he said.

title: 'Respect your neighbors' - Caroline Commission passes temporary moratorium on DAF storage
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
'Respect your neighbors' - Caroline Commission passes temporary moratorium on DAF storage

 December 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: A1 | Section: News 
 
 1013
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - The Caroline County Commissioners upheld a resolution introduced at their Dec. 12 meeting, but only after revising some language in a temporary moratorium on DAF storage in the county.Following what was at times a contentious, nearly two-hour debate among local residents and poultry industry representatives from out of state, the three commissioners adjourned to go into closed session to further refine the resolution for another 90 minutes.
About 30 people attended the 9 a.m. meeting, and chairs had to be brought in to accommodate them in the small meeting room in the Caroline County Courthouse.
The commissioners adopted Resolution 2023-025 as a "temporary moratorium on certain use of land or structures for storage of food processing residual and/or DAF residuals in Caroline County" for 60 days, starting Dec. 19.
However, the moratorium doesn't apply to structures or land used for storage of those residuals prior to Jan. 1, 2023.
"In other words, we're not addressing the legality or not of such facilities," County Attorney Stewart Barroll said. "We are stating that future uses of land or structures are subject to the moratorium. So, this does not directly attack a preexisting facility." The poultry byproduct treatment system in question is dissolved air flotation, otherwise known as DAF.
A DAF pit is located on River Road outside Ridgely.
At the Dec. 12 Commission meeting, neighbors living near the pit reported the stench and flies emanating from the open-pit DAF were unlike manure since the DAF contains poultry processing byproducts.
Although it does not own that DAF storage tank, three representatives of the Arkansas-based Denali Corporation, "a specialty waste and environmental services company," according to its website, attended the meeting. They requested a 60-to 90-day delay in enacting the moratorium.
The company operates on Delmarva and "specialize (s) in repurposing DAF skimmings, transforming them into nutrient-rich soil amendments." Denali attorney Mark Cropper requested the delay, citing the holiday season and only having a few hours to review the resolution.
"I don't think there is an urgency that necessitates a moratorium," Cropper said.
"But I fully welcome and fully support the investigation you want to undertake." Several attendees who live on River Road, Cedar Lane and Peaviner Road alluded to the "one bad actor," whose River Road operation contains openair DAF holding tanks that produce a stench and flies, negatively affecting neighbors' quality of life.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter asked several times, "If there are ways to control the odor and the flies, why hasn't it been done?" Glenn Dowling, a senior environmental manager with Denali Water Solutions in Georgia, said Denali can respond to a problem when they are made aware of it. He said he would appreciate a "60-to 90-day reprieve" for "time to help create a solution that could become a model for the future." Barroll challenged the Denali representatives. "I'm a little curious that you're surprised by the complaints about odor and fly infestation, when Denali's been sued in multiple states in the last several years for exactly that. And you sit here telling us you didn't have any idea that that was happening here." The commissioners reiterated several times that their main concern was how DAF residuals from the Delmarva poultry industry are stored, not how they are applied.
They also reiterated their concern that materials are trucked into the county, stressing county road infrastructure.
They questioned why the poultry processing plants were not building DAF storage on the sites of their plants.
Dowling called the timing of the resolution "pretty curious." "Because it's being considered at the inception of the 2023-2024 winter nutrient application ban in Maryland and Delaware, it's difficult to accommodate when that storage of those materials is essential to the continuity of service of businesses," Dowling said. "It is allowed by the state (of Maryland) to store those materials specifically to protect natural resources and water resources on the Eastern Shore." The purpose of the temporary moratorium is to give the commissioners time to research the issue of DAF storage and "enact appropriate legislation." "I want to make it clear that I am pro-ag, but this needs to be cleaned up," Commission President Travis Breeding said.
Addressing his remarks to the poultry industry representatives, he said, "You need to carry that message back that we are not going to have this go on in our county. This does not mean that I'm not willing to vote to put a moratorium on the entire operation because, frankly, I am. But I think we need to sit down at the table.
It needs to be addressed, and we need to be a part of it. And the citizens of this county need to be a part of it, and they need to be heard by the producers, by the haulers and by the applicators." The Maryland Department of Agriculture "needs to be doing a better job, but they don't have to do a better job; if the applicators do a better job, then we don't have as many complaints," Breeding said. "So, stick to the regulations and make sure that they're enforced." The resolution also stated that county staff, Boards and Commissions are directed and requested to act in a manner consistent with the provisions of the moratorium." "We have directed staff to prioritize enforcement of our permitting process on non-permitted structures at this point," Breeding said.
"I'm ready to put the clamps on, so you guys need to come to the table," Commissioner Frank Bartz said.
"And respect your neighbors.
Respect this community," Breeding said.
A public hearing on the subject of the moratorium will be held 6 p.m. Tuesday, Jan. 23, in Room 111 of the Health and Public Service Building (HAPS), 403 S. 7th St., Denton.

 DENTON — Greensboro Historic Society President Charles Dean has a vision for the Caroline County Courthouse's new door. "About a month after that, there was an architect by the name of William Buckland, and he presented designs for the very first Caroline County Courthouse."
The County Commissioners have been having conversations about a new courthouse door since December, when security concerns at the facility were brought to their attention. The conversation came up after Circuit Court Judge Heather Price said she had been receiving death threats. Price declined to comment further on the matter at this time.
The county approved the budget for installing new windows at the building in December but tabled the conversation about the door, raising concerns with historical accuracy.
The Caroline County Courthouse is a historical site in Denton. According to the Greensboro Historical Society, the courthouse was first built in 1797 and then was rebuilt in 1895. The courthouse was redesigned in 1965 to what it looks like today.
Dean sent an email to Caroline County Commissioners explaining the history of the courthouse. He believes that the county is not going back far enough in time with its research for the new door.
"My email to the commissioners basically reiterated these facts," Dean said. "I'm not sure that they have ever seen pictures of the original courthouse door or the second courthouse door. They're going for a replica of the current courthouse door. So if they wanted to be historically accurate, they could go back much further than 1965."
Caroline County shares the courthouse with several state departments, and certain security protocols need to be followed. The county commissioners are committed to keeping the courthouse's historic design, as long as this is in keeping with state mandates.
"Let's see what Mr. Dean has," Commission President Travis Breeding said at the commissioners' Tuesday meeting. "If its a picture or a design."
The grant cycle has passed for the county to get funding for the door, but the commissioners decided Tuesdays that the door can be paid for with county funds.
"We will find someone to get the information and give it to facilities and look at the historic door," Breeding said. "If we don't like the historic door, we will get the door replaced."

title: Let's let county election officials do their job
author: Staff Writer
content:
Let's let county election officials do their job

 October 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 730
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Talbot County Board of Elections received some high-level backing — and vindication — this week. The Maryland attorney general and the state administrator of elections both backed the work and processes used to ensure fair elections in the county.Recently local election officials must have felt they were under siege. First a county council member called for the County Council to send a letter to the elections board reminding Election Director Tammy Stafford and the elections board to follow state law.
Days later county Sheriff Joe Gamble sent the board a letter strongly urging them to follow state law.
This comes against a continuing drumbeat of challenges by Talbot County residents that has been ongoing for most of this year.
The word from on high: Back off, there is nothing being done that violates state law.
Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown wrote a letter to Gamble detailing the "limited role of local law enforcement, including our sheriff's office in the electoral process."
The letter from Brown was read aloud by Stafford during an Oct. 7 Board of Elections special meeting.
Although the letter is not an official opinion of the attorney general, Brown said he hopes the letter is helpful in setting forth the roles of law enforcement officers during elections.
The letter is the latest salvo on the topic of sometimes tense back-and-forth between the Talbot County Board of Elections, the Talbot County sheriff and local elected officials in recent weeks.
In Brown's letter, he addresses the role of law enforcement, security, authority on election law violations and concerns involving election judges.
"State law does, specifies and carefully circumscribes the authority of local law enforcement and polling places while conferring primary responsibility for election law enforcement on other agencies," Brown said. "I understand that local law enforcement agencies do provide assistance to local boards of elections in some jurisdictions, including deploying personnel to provide security and transporting election materials. But importantly, this is done at the request and under the direction of the local Board of Elections itself."
Gamble's letter came in the midst of intense discussions centering concerns over the partisan breakdown of election judges ahead of the Nov. 5 General Election.
According to the most recent breakdown from the Talbot County Board of Elections, 62 judges are Democrats, 50 are Republicans and 11 are unaffiliated.
Maryland election code states "each polling place shall have an equal number of election judges" from "the majority party" and "the principal minority party."
Discussion about the imbalance of election judge political party affiliations surfaced after Talbot County Council Member Dave Stepp raised it in a council meeting Sept. 24. He voiced concerns the county Board of Elections was not following state law for election judges, though his motion for the council to send a letter to the elections board failed by a 2-3 vote.
In his letter, Brown emphasized state law "does not require equality in the total number of judges" recruited and trained by the local Board of Elections.
"Even at the individual polling place level, while all local boards make best efforts to achieve exact party balance, this is not always possible for reasons outside the local board's control, including the number of judges from each party who volunteer," Brown said.
Toward the end of Brown's letter, he advised that opening a polling place, even if the number of judges from each party is not exactly equal, is preferable to "closing the polling place and disenfranchising all the voters who would have voted there."
The week prior, Jared DeMarinis, the state administrator of elections, released a statement regarding the assignment of election judges. In it, he emphasized that Maryland voters should feel "confident" in the state's election security and "compliance with the law."
"An election judge's partisan affiliation does not impact or determine the outcome of the election," DeMarinis wrote. "Voters decide the outcomes of elections. The party affiliation of an election judge does not stop them from casting their ballots or disenfranchise a voter. And to say otherwise is disingenuous."
DeMarinis noted in his statement the strict rules election judges must follow, binding them "to conduct the election in a nonpartisan manner and fashion."
With these statements of support by top level state officials, we hope that the seemingly partisan attacks on the integrity of Talbot County elections can end. County election officials have a big job ahead of them — ensuring the smooth and secure election ahead on Nov. 5. Let's let them do their job.

Deputies responded to the store when a call went out that a theft had occurred.
According to a sheriff's office report, "Two males and one female entered the store and placed numerous colognes and perfumes into bags and fled the store. After fleeing the store, witnesses observed all three suspects enter a gray Mercury Montego that fled northbound on Route 4."
According to court documents filed by Deputy Antonio Tavares, Deputy Justin MacWilliams located the Mercury traveling northbound on Route 4, which then turned onto Route 2.
MacWilliams "initiated a traffic stop in the area of Pushaw Station Road in Sunderland. During the traffic stop, five occupants were located in the suspect vehicle along with numerous bags of perfumes and colognes in plain view. The total value of the stolen items was approximately $7,694 dollars."
In addition to the merchandise that was allegedly stolen from the Prince Frederick store, Tavares reported in charging papers that several cellphones were also confiscated.
The five arrested are identified as Yeiner Jose Rodriguez Barcelo, 27, of Bronx, N.Y., Yoncar Alberto Rainoso, 21, of Manhattan, N.Y., Estefani Andrea Urbano-Zapata, 21, of Cape Girardea, Mo., Raimil Marquez Jimenez, 25, of Washington, D.C., and Adony Josue Carana, 27, of Manhattan N.Y.

title: Man gets three life sentences for double murder
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Man gets three life sentences for double murder

 July 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 1084
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A man who gunned down a woman and her boyfriend inside an abandoned house near North East in July 2023 before stealing their cell phones received three consecutive life sentences — plus 35 additional years — on Monday, one day before the second anniversary of the double murder.The defendant — Richard L. Stone, 46, of Aberdeen — fatally shot Christopher Blaine Thomas, 46, in his chest and Thomas' cohabiting girlfriend, Ashley Dove Brown, five times on July 1, 2023 inside the bedroom of an abandoned house in the 100 block of Bethel Church Road.
Shot in the chest, abdomen, thigh, arm and wrist, Brown was murdered on her 34th birthday.
Stone's co-defendant — Jordan Patrick Perry, 28, of Elkton — is scheduled to be sentenced on July 14. Perry is facing three life sentences and a significant humber of additional years after a jury convicted him of two counts of first-degree murder and 31 related charges on May 1 at the conclusion of a four-day-long trial, after deliberating about 90 minutes.
"I hope you both rot in Hades and that God . . . not . . . have . . . mercy . . . on . . . your . . . souls," Jerry Brown, the father of Ashley Brown, remarked Monday during his victim impact statement while standing at a courtroom podium a few feet away from Stone, seated at the defense table in a jail uniform.
Brown purposely left pregnant pauses between the last few words of his comment for emphasis. Brown told the judge that he still cries frequently over the senseless taking of his daughter's life. "They murdered a big part of me," he said.
Moments earlier, his 64-year-old wife, Bonnie Brown, who discovered the bodies of her daughter and Thomas, commented, "I have a life sentence of PTSD, and they have shown no remorse," during her victim-impact statement in the courtroom. (The Browns have been married for 38 years.)
Thomas' surviving family members also read victim-impact statements with similar sentiments aloud in the courtroom, including his mother and son, who listed his high school graduation and his senior walk off the football field as some of the milestones that his murdered father missed. Thomas' daughter submitted a written victim-impact statement to the judge and appeared on courtroom screen via Zoom.
Assistant State's Attorney Scott Lewis described the murders of Brown and Thomas as a "very senseless crime" while making his sentence recommendation. Lewis also told the judge that he is still taken aback by the "brutality of it," noting that bullets lethally damaged the hearts of both victims and that the fatal gunshot for Brown was fired while she was prone on the floor, already wounded.
"What compassion was shown? Where is the sense of humanity?" Lewis asked rhetorically.
Cecil County Circuit Court Judge William W. Davis Jr. imposed sentences on Stone that matched Lewis' recommendation.
Davis imposed a life sentence on Stone for first-degree murder relating to Brown; a consecutive life sentence for first-degree murder relating to Thomas; and a consecutive life sentence for conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.
In addition, the judge imposed a consecutive 25-year sentence on Stone for home invasion and then suspended 15 years of the penalty, leaving Stone with an additional 10 years of incarceration.
Davis also imposed two consecutive 20-year sentences on Stone for armed robbery and use of a handgun in the commission of a felony or a crime of violence, before suspending 10 years of each of those penalties. The judge noted that the use-of-a-handgun conviction carries a mandatory five-year sentence.
On April 4, at the conclusion of a four-day-long trial, a jury deliberated approximately five hours before convicting Stone of all 45 charges against him. The majority of those convictions merged into other convictions during Monday's sentencing.
Stone maintained his innocence at sentencing and, through his defense lawyer, Michael J. Halter, he indicated that he planned to file an appeal.
Prefacing that Stone does not lack "sympathy and empathy," Halter told the judge, "He had nothing to do with this crime. He has been adamant since Day One that he did not participate in these crimes."
Halter noted that Stone's convicted co-defendant, Perry, had "a grudge with Thomas over a drug sale" and that Stone had had no interactions with Thomas.
The defense lawyer stressed that, on the morning of the double murder, Stone unwittingly accompanied Perry and one other man in a convoy from their Aberdeen residence to the abandoned house where Brown and Thomas were living.
(Brown and Thomas were recovering drug addicts, and they had been squatting in that abandoned house with boarded-up windows and no electricity for approximately eight months, according to trial testimony, which indicated that Thomas sometimes borrowed a generator to power the place.)
"He (Stone) was with them, but he did not know what they were going to do. He was at the wrong place at the wrong time with the wrong people," Halter assertively summarized.
Halter asked the judge to run the sentences concurrently, opining that, otherwise, Stone would have "no possibility to see the light of day."
Stone stood at the defense table and maintained his innocence during his allocution, telling the judge, "The events that happened, I had no part in it. No life should be (taken)."
From the bench, Davis reminded Stone that the jury had spoken.
The judge reviewed that the evidence that Cecil County Sheriff's Office detectives, deputies and crime-scene technicians collected included Stone's registered handgun — one of firearms used in the double murder — and that it had Stone's DNA on it. (Investigators recovered the stolen cell phones belonging to Brown and Thomas inside Perry's bedroom, in the same Aberdeen house were Stone was living.) Incriminating text messages also were gathered.
Collected evidence also included distinctive masks matching those described by an eyewitness who saw an unmasked Perry accompanied by masked men on that Bethel Church Road property on the morning of July 1, 2023. Moments after that group arrived on a motorcycle and in a car, the eyewitness heard someone kick in the front door of the abandoned house, a scream and then a gunshot, which prompted him to run into the wood in fear.
In addition, the judge reviewed that CCSO investigators had tracked down several videos gleaned from security-cameras between Aberdeen and North East and that those videos showed Stone traveling in that caravan to that Bethel Church Road property on the morning of the double murder and directly after it occurred.
"It's hard not to listen to the jury and to what the (surviving) family (members) said," Davis told Stone from the bench.

title: Oxford commission approves changes to floodplain management
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado

Oxford commission approves changes to floodplain management

 October 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News

 OXFORD — The Commissioners of Oxford approved an ordinance to amend the town's floodplain management ordinance. The changes would loosen requirements for residents seeking to make significant improvements to buildings.Commission President Norm Bell opened the public hearing for Ordinance 2416 and shared additional information on the changes made.
Previously for buildings in Oxford, owners were required to track and calculate the costs of any construction made since July 1, 2013 prior to making changes to the structures.
If all those improvement costs equal or exceed 50% of the market value of a building prior to the start of the construction, it would require the building to be up to code and raised in elevation.
The amended ordinance revises the definition of "substantial improvement," removing the 2013 date and substituting "the previous five (5) years."
Bell said the revision allows for a lean way for owners to make improvements on their buildings.
"What this is saying is we're only going to go back five years, or 1,825 days," Bell said. "So it's shortening the period that you can take a look at the 50% requirement. It's liberalizing it."
An additional change in the ordinance was the revision of the "agreement to submit an elevation certificate."
An elevation certificate is a form on which applicants for a permit to construct a building or structure show compliance with floodplain management legislation.
Previously people looking to make substantial improvements to buildings would need to submit an elevation certificate with a building permit application upon the construction of the foundation and prior to further vertical construction; and prior to the final inspection and moving in.
The revision removes the requirement of submitting the form prior to placement of the foundation and further vertical construction.
According to Bell, the changes would make it cheaper for owners to have engineers/surveyors certify that the floor of buildings seeking improvements is above the mean high water mark and it lowers costs of the certification by a "couple of hundred dollars."
After answering clarifying questions from the public, commissioners unanimously approved the ordinance.

 CHESTERTOWN — A Chestertown pediatrician has surrendered his license to practice in Maryland ahead of a civil case filed Tuesday morning in Kent County Circuit Court.Julio Ramirez, formerly head of his private practice at 6602 Church Hill Road in Chestertown, is being sued by a Kent County woman. The woman, who is not named in court filings, is seeking relief from the court for physical, psychological and emotional injuries she said she incurred while seeking treatment for her child in his office in 2023.
According to court documents, the woman was touched inappropriately and in a sexual manner while in the treatment room with Ramirez and her daughter. Following the encounter, which she said she tried to rebuff, the woman notified office staff and subsequently filed a report with the Chestertown Police Department.
In September 2023, the woman made a formal complaint to the Maryland State Board of Physicians.
Through the course of the board's investigation, four former employees "all testified to a pervasive environment of sexually abusive, unethical, and inappropriate behavior," according to the investigation report.
The investigation found Ramirez, on multiple occasions, sexually assaulted at least three female employees of his over the course of several years. The investigation further found that he sexually assaulted at least one other mother while in the course of treating her child.
Following the board's initial inquiry into the allegations in April, the board ordered a summary suspension of Ramirez's license, concluding "the public health, safety or welfare imperatively required emergency action in this case."
As a result of the board's investigation, Ramirez permanently surrendered his license to practice medicine, according to a letter Ramirez sent to the board.
As listed by the Maryland Board of Physicians, Ramirez, 65, graduated from Universidad de El Salvador Facultad de Medicina in 1988. He was first licensed in Maryland in 1998.

 CAMBRIDGE — In an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit, the Dorchester County Council introduced a draft fiscal year 2026 budget that raised taxes.The $91.96 million proposed operating budget presented Tuesday includes proposals to increase property taxes, remove the municipal tax differential, increase local income tax and eliminate tax rebates offered to municipalities.
The council will consider these proposals through the remainder of the budget process, which concludes May 20.
The balanced draft budget comes after months of work by county staff to eliminate an estimated $6.2 million operating budget deficit, which the county has said was brought on by cost shifts from the state.
"These are painful decisions," County Manager Jerry Jones said in an interview with The Star Democrat. "But at the end of the day, given the climate and what's being pushed down from the state for us to absorb, sadly it's one of those things we have to do."
GETTING INTO THE NUMBERS
In the draft operating budget, the county is proposing an increase of the real property tax by 3 cents so county residents would pay a rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed valuation of property.
The proposal to remove the tax differential, or lower property tax rate, for municipalities would mean Cambridge and Hurlock residents would have to pay the full tax rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed valuation of property.
In the current fiscal year, Cambridge residents pay the county $0.9267 per $100 of assessed valuation of property and Hurlock residents pay $0.9179 per $100 of assessed value.
On properties with a semi-annual tax payment option, the proposal would add a service charge based on a rate of 0.02% applied to unpaid real property taxes due in December.
With the proposed property tax changes to the budget, the county expects to bring in an additional $2.15 million.
The proposed budget would raise the county's income tax rate from 3.2% to 3.3%, generating $600,000 more in revenue.
In another effort to increase revenue, the county voted April 15 to increase its 911 fee to $4.25 per month. This is the second time the rate has been raised this year.
In early March, the council passed a resolution to increase the county fee that residents pay on their cell phone lines from $1.50 to $2 per month. Council Vice President Mike Detmer said in March that he introduced the legislation to increase the fee to $4.25 as a potential way to reduce a budget deficit.
To alleviate the tax and fee increases' impact on seniors, the county is considering expanding its senior tax credit, which offers a 5% deduction on the county tax bill for those who are at least 70 years old and receive the Homeowners' Property Tax Credit. If passed, the expansion would increase that deduction to 10% and expand eligibility to Homeowners' Property Tax Credit recipients who are at least 67 years old.
Proposed expenditure increases include 3% salary increases for airport, solid waste, water and wastewater, courthouse maintenance, courthouse security and Eastern Shore Innovation Center personnel and an increase in spending on the county's 14 volunteer fire companies. The proposed $35,000 total increase to fire companies would add to the county's $1.22 million expenditure on fire companies and advanced life support services.
Proposed cuts to expenditures include the delaying or eliminating funding to nonprofits that request money from the county.
According to the draft grants budget, the county expects to receive a total of $9.78 million in state and federal grants.
At the end of the council meeting April 15, Detmer encouraged residents to come to council meetings or reach out to council members and make their voices and concerns about the budget heard. He said he is available to discuss the budget or just listen.
"It's your budget too," he said.
The first public budget hearing, as well as a meeting with municipalities, will be held May 6.

 ANNAPOLIS - An audit released Friday found that the Maryland Board of Elections did not report for more than a year its findings that people voted or tried to vote more than once in the 2020 general election - well after the results were certified, according to The Office of Legislative Audits.The state elections board identified 134 voters who voted more than once and 1,371 voters who attempted to vote multiple times in the 2020 general election, but it did not report these individuals to the The Office of State Prosecutor until April 2022, the audit said. The audit is part of a routine physical compliance audit of the SBE conducted every three to four years."Definitely the (reports) for the 2020 general election were significantly late and I think they indicated that was due to staff turnover within their office," said Matthew Streett, an assistant director for the Compliance and Performance Audit Division of the OLA. "They reported them after the election results were certified." In the July 2022 primary election, the audit found, the elections board identified four individuals who successfully voted multiple times and 263 voters who attempted to vote multiple times, referring the information to the state prosecutors office in a "timely" manner.Election integrity has become a high-profile issue with former President Donald Trump and his supporters repeatedly challenging the outcome of the 2020 presidential election.The audit also noted that the elections board could enhance its procedures to fully identify deceased or duplicate voters. The audit identified 2,426 "potentially deceased individuals" whose voter registrations were active and 327 individuals with potential duplicate voter registrations."We're just pointing out areas where they can improve," said Streett. "The information they're getting from the Maryland Department of Health was not fully complete and accurate, so they were missing out on a certain pocket of deceased individuals." The Health Department could not be reached for comment on Friday.The audit also found deficiencies with the state elections board's security and control over its information systems, but did not go into detail for security reasons. The department's response to those concerns also was redacted from the report.The elections board did agree to implement the recommendations, but disagreed with several findings.The State Board of Elections could not be reached for comment on Friday.The current Elections Administrator Jared DeMarinis took the helm in June 2023 after longtime administrator Linda Lamone retired.

 OCEAN CITY — Solar energy was one topic of discussion that captured the attention of multiple Mid-Shore counties at the Maryland Association of Counties Summer Conference.Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding said solar energy came up a lot at the four-day conference, which went from Aug. 14 to Aug. 17 in Ocean City. Breeding said there are elected officials from different Maryland counties who feel that solar lobbyists are pushing the state to take away local authority when it comes to where solar energy system sites can go and how close those sites can be from roads and neighboring structures.
Caroline County currently has a 2,000-acre cap on solar projects. Once that limit is reached, the county will stop permitting new solar energy system projects on county land, Breeding said.
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said his fellow council member Ricky Travers asked about solar site acreage caps in a MACo session with the Maryland Public Service Commission. Specifically, Travers asked about how the commission feels about these caps.
Pfeffer said that after the session, the Dorchester County Council members had a conversation with Public Service Commissioner Kumar Barve, and the council was able to explain its concerns about increasing solar sites in the county. Pfeffer said the only part of the county that can host these sites is the north part of the county, and that is where the council hopes to grow the county's tax base.
"They were very interested and didn't realize some of the demographics and logistics of Dorchester County," Pfeffer said about the Public Service Commission. "So I'm hoping that is successful for us, they'll take a look at it and they won't establish any legislation that's one-size-fits-all."
Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher called the conference one of the best he's been to. He said it ran smoothly and was well put together.
Breeding said that MACo's summer and winter conferences give Maryland counties an opportunity to get together, discuss and "try to come up with a unified message."
"It was a good conference," Breeding said. "We got to talk to all of our partners in other counties, bounce ideas off of them, discuss problems and issues that we're all facing and kind of brainstorm on how to resolve those issues."
Pfeffer, who is the secretary of MACo this year, said that all counties have problems.
Pfeffer said the opportunity to discuss these common problems, no matter how many zeros come after them, can benefit each county.
Breeding said he is taking some ideas on solar power back home to Caroline County this year. He talked about the systems that Talbot and Queen Anne's counties have in place, including Talbot County's point system that is used to help preserve prime farmland for farming and determine where solar sites can go.
Lesher said he didn't attend the solar session at MACo, but said the Talbot County Council tackled legislation dealing with solar energy sites last year when it put the point system in place.
"Which I think is model legislation for other rural jurisdictions," he said. "Right now we're in the testing period for this. Will this hold up? "After Elien was shot and lying on the driveway with life threatening injuries," Kane allegedly took "something off Elien" and ran away, per court records.

Charging documents show police identified Kane and Johnson through video footage. Johnson was also identified during witness interviews, court records state.

Ross Benincasa, who is senior vice president of community development at Chesapeake Community Development, a subsidiary of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, said the demolition will take six months. He said some of the material from the silos will be salvaged for potential future use.
Although demolition has begun, the project still requires site plan approval from the Easton Planning Commission. It is scheduled to go before the Planning Commission on Thursday. Following site plan approval, the project will need standard grading and building permits.
Easton resident Maury Schlesinger was walking his dog Monday when he noticed demolition was underway. Although he has some concerns with future plans for the site, Schlesinger said he thinks the demolition is "appropriate."
"Something has to happen there," he said.
According to the draft site plan for Easton Crossing, if approved, the development would create 123 multi-family units, including 29 affordable apartments priced below the market rate. It would also bring parking, stormwater management and landscaping to the property.
The property would have six buildings, with some buildings that include commercial spaces. The first building, which would have 15 units, is expected to open in December 2027 if the plan is approved.

"I think it needs to be relooked at," he said.

title: Mental Health experts offer tips for managing New Year's resolutions
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Mental Health experts offer tips for managing New Year's resolutions

 January 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 585
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The new year is here, and what comes with it, for many people, is a fresh start.New Year's resolutions are infamously tied to failure of goals, but mental health experts share that if people are seeking positive change in their lives, understanding mental health will allow people to not only accomplish their goals but to be kinder to themselves if they are unable to achieve their goals within an expected time frame.
Katie Theeke, vice president of marketing and communications at For All Seasons, said the connection between mental health and New Year's resolutions are heavily tied together.
"Mental health is foundational to how we think, feel and act," Theeke said. "When we care for our mental health we feel better, and people will often see their quality of life and relationships improve. Without awareness and care for our mental health, it's very difficult to have the motivation and commitment to fulfill our hopes and goals for the new year."
According to Centerstone, a national nonprofit specializing in mental health and substance use disorder, there is an unspoken rule that resolutions should be all or nothing extremities. This mindset it often leads to difficult-to-accomplish resolutions and then ideas of self-sabotage and punishment if resolutions are not accomplished, Centerstone said.
Theeke said it is great to think of goals, but what is more important is the little steps and systems that are put into place to steer people in the direction they want to go. Instead of focusing on a big goal like losing a significant amount of weight, she encourages people to try to set up a simple system to start getting healthy, such as walking with a friend each week.
Theeke said it's the small attainable steps that start to build up. If one system doesn't work it's important to evaluate and change the system to something that works better for the individual.
For those who want to make resolutions around mental health, Theeke suggests considering activities that bring positive emotions, whether it be music, walking, exercising, feeding and watching birds, or spending time with friends and family. Prioritizing simple acts of joy, even if it requires carving time out to do so, can have big gains in mental health growth, she said.
For those who find themselves continuing to feel low for more than two weeks at a time, Theeke suggests considering reaching out to a mental health professional. Individuals need to take the time to invest in themselves and investing in mental health can have lasting gains.
But most importantly, Theeke encourages everyone to be kind to themselves regardless of success on their resolutions. If people are able to approach themselves with more kindness and understanding, it can help build the confidence needed to accomplish whatever goals that are made. But most importantly, kindness for self can make moving forward with everyday life easier and improve personal relationships.
"One of the nicest things you can do for yourself in the new year is change your internal dialogue," Theeke said. "So many of us are criticizing ourselves throughout the day. Catch yourself if you are thinking something negative and try out some simple phrases like, 'I am focusing on progress, not perfection.' Or, 'I am getting a little stronger and healthier every day.' There are so many positive affirmations out there. Find a few that feel right for you and try them. Reach out to a trusted friend or a mental health professional if you continue to struggle. There are good people out there who are ready to help."
